articles.body_html:
If you have ever tried to create custom street-art lettering or a stylized wordmark for a poster, sticker, avatar, or side-project logo, you usually run into two frustrating extremes:

  1. Static .ttf graffiti fonts feel robotic. Standard font files lock every character onto a rigid horizontal baseline with uniform kerning. Worse, repeated letters look identical, and you cannot easily tilt a single glyph, scale up the first letter, or control how thick outlines overlap without converting text to outlines in desktop vector software first.
  2. AI image generators are a black box for typography. Prompt-based generators create cool raster scenes, but they still struggle with exact character spelling, bake the background into the pixels, and give you zero control when you simply want to nudge the third letter up by 10px or export clean vector <path> geometry.

That gap is why I built Graffitizer — a free, browser-based graffiti lettering studio designed to bridge the gap between a quick font generator and a full vector editor.

👉 Try it live here: https://www.graffitizer.com/ (Free to use, no account required, no watermarks)

Why Deterministic Presets + Per-Letter Manipulation Beat Prompts

Instead of generating flat raster images from AI prompts, Graffitizer uses deterministic font shapes paired with layered style presets that you can manipulate directly on an interactive canvas.

When you type a name, nickname, or short phrase (up to 20 characters, supporting English letters, numbers, supported punctuation, and Chinese characters), the studio treats every character as an independent, editable object rather than a static text string.

Approach Spelling Accuracy Per-Letter Transform & Overlap True Transparent Cutout Editable Vector Paths (SVG)
Standard .ttf Font Generators High No (fixed baseline & kerning) Sometimes Rarely (requires font installation)
AI Prompt Generators Unpredictable No (requires re-prompting) Requires background removal No (raster pixels only)
Graffitizer 100% Deterministic Yes (move, rotate, resize, layer) Yes (1-click Transparent PNG) Yes (English glyphs exported as SVG paths)

Key Features Under the Hood

1. Three Core Street-Art Styles & 90 Curated Presets

A blank canvas can be intimidating, so Graffitizer starts with 90 curated presets split evenly across three foundational graffiti styles:

  • Bubble Graffiti (30 Presets): Rounded, playful letterforms with bold outlines and high-contrast fills that stay legible at any size.

  • Graffiti Tags (30 Presets): Marker-inspired handstyles designed for short nicknames and slanted signatures, including presets like Original Marker, Dry Marker, Chalk Scratch, Street Scrawl, Mist Tag, Wet Paint Tag, and Neon Halo Tag.

  • Wildstyle Graffiti (30 Presets): Sharper geometry, multi-layered outlines, and decorative effects such as Neon Handstyle, Chrome Tag, Paint Drip, Electric Signature, Gold Rush, Double Outline Tag, and Bevel.

Switching between presets updates the visual styling while preserving your typed text so you can compare directions in seconds.

2. Independent Per-Letter Canvas Controls

In real graffiti lettering, rhythm comes from breaking uniformity. On the Graffitizer canvas, a preset is just your starting point:

  • Direct Canvas Manipulation: Click or tap any character to drag its position, pull corner handles to resize it, or use the top handle to rotate its angle.
  • Independent Repeated Characters: If your word has repeated letters (like the two As in LAILA or LUNA), each instance remains completely separate—scaling, tilting, or recoloring one character never mutates the other.
  • Layer & Overlap Management: When bold outlines overlap, you can reorder letter layers to control which glyph sits in front, or undo an adjustment immediately if an overlap hurts readability.
  • Granular Color & Background Control: Recolor individual letters, apply a cohesive style palette across all glyphs at once, pick a solid canvas background, or upload your own custom background image to preview the lettering in context.

Here is how the exact same word (LUNA) and preset look before and after individual per-letter adjustments:

Before (Starting Preset):

After (Per-Letter Position, Rotation, Scale & Color Adjustments):

3. Real-World Use Cases & Production-Ready Exports (PNG, Transparent PNG, SVG)

Whether you are dropping a wordmark onto a YouTube thumbnail, printing a notebook sticker, or refining curves in Figma or Illustrator, Graffitizer exports artwork directly from the browser without watermarks or signups:

  • PNG (With Background): Exports a ready-to-use image with your chosen canvas background color or uploaded backdrop included.
  • Transparent PNG: Strips the background cleanly so you can layer your lettering over posters, slides, or social profile graphics.
  • SVG (Vector Shapes): Exports your design as scalable vector artwork. English letters are converted directly into vector <path> shapes rather than <text> dependencies—meaning you can open the .svg in any vector editor without installing a single font file.

Here are a few ways the exported lettering can be used in real projects:

  • Name Stickers (LAILA): Export a transparent PNG with a bold outline to place over physical or digital labels.

  • Avatar Wordmarks (ACE): Pair a short nickname with a 1:1 square canvas for a high-contrast profile graphic.

  • Event & Poster Titles (OPEN MIC): Export custom wildstyle lettering and layer it directly over your poster photography.

4. Built-In Aspect Ratios & Mobile-Friendly Precision

To save time resizing exports later, the editor includes one-click canvas aspect ratios alongside custom pixel dimensions:

  • Original: 1600 × 840
  • Square (1:1): 1080 × 1080 (ideal for avatars and profile wordmarks)
  • Classic & Portrait (4:3 / 3:4 / 3:2): 1200 × 900, 900 × 1200, and 1500 × 1000
  • Widescreen & Vertical (16:9 / 9:16): 1920 × 1080 and 1080 × 1920
  • Touch + Precision Controls: On smaller mobile screens where finger-dragging can feel cramped, dedicated position controls let you nudge individual letters with pixel-level accuracy.

Zero-Friction Philosophy: Client-Side & Privacy-First

One of my biggest pet peeves with online creative tools is spending ten minutes customizing a design only to hit a paywall, watermark, or mandatory email signup modal on the download button.

As noted on our SideProjectors project page, Graffitizer was built to stay completely frictionless:

  • No accounts or onboarding walls: Open the page, type a word, and export immediately.
  • Ephemeral session state: All edits happen live in your current browser tab—nothing is stored on a backend account, and refreshing gives you a clean slate.

Calling for Feedback from the Dev.to Community!

I would love for you to take Graffitizer for a spin and let me know what you think:

  1. UX & Canvas Controls: Does dragging, rotating, and layering individual letters feel intuitive on your device (desktop or mobile)?
  2. SVG Export Workflow: If you import the exported .svg paths into Figma, Illustrator, or Inkscape, how does the path structure hold up for your workflow?
  3. Preset Wish List: Which new style presets, text effects, or export options would you want to see added next?

Drop your thoughts, critiques, or your favorite lettering creations in the comments below!

articles.title: What I Look for Before Trusting an AI App Builder With a Real Project
articles.description: AI app builders can now generate a working database, authentication flow, and deployed URL from a...
articles.body_html:
AI app builders can now generate a working database, authentication flow, and deployed URL from a natural-language prompt. But a convincing demo is only the beginning: what happens when real users, permissions, and persistent data enter the picture?

I went looking for a concrete answer by digging into Floot, a YC-backed AI app builder that plugs into Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor as an MCP connector, since it's one of the more recent entrants making a specific architectural claim: that bundling the whole stack (backend, database, hosting, auth) into one AI-native framework produces more reliable output than tools that bolt AI onto existing dev services.

I haven't built a production app with Floot myself, so I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I can offer is a framework: the specific things I'd want answered, with sources, before handing any AI app builder, Floot or otherwise, a real project. If you've used Floot or a competitor for something beyond a prototype, I'd genuinely like to hear where this framework holds up and where it doesn't.

How Floot's workflow actually works

Worth establishing first, since the architecture is the whole pitch, and it's worth getting precise about which architecture, because Floot actually ships two.

The one most of the current marketing leads with is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) connector: instead of a separate web app, you add Floot to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or another MCP client, and build from inside that chat. Floot's own documentation is specific about who does what here: your assistant creates the project, writes the files, provisions the database, runs the app, reads its own errors, and publishes, each as a direct tool call against your project. Floot's role in this path is the infrastructure underneath (a managed Postgres database, auth, file storage, hosting), not a second layer of AI reviewing the first one's work. Whatever model you're already paying for (Claude, GPT) is the one doing the interpreting, writing, and debugging.

That's a meaningfully different claim than the one I originally saw repeated across older coverage of Floot, which describes a three-pass system: one AI interprets the request, a second writes the code, and a first or third reviews and fixes it. That description is real, but it traces back to Floot's original standalone product, the in-app editor with its own built-in AI agent, which Floot still offers as a separate path alongside the connector. If you're building through the MCP connector, which is the model this article is mostly about, that multi-pass review isn't the mechanism in play; your own assistant's single pass, including its own error-reading, is.

That distinction matters for how much scrutiny to apply. Without a second, independent AI layer checking the first one's work in the connector flow, the self-correction loop is a single model catching its own mistakes, not two systems cross-checking each other. Whether that's reliable in practice, on a non-trivial app, is the kind of thing only hands-on use will tell you.

The six things I'd actually test

This is the part I think is missing from most AI-builder coverage: a list of claims to verify, not a verdict. If you're evaluating Floot (or Bolt, Lovable, Replit, Base44) for something real, these are the specific things I'd check before trusting the output, not just the marketing page.

What to test Why it matters
User isolation A high-impact failure mode to test for: create two accounts and check whether either can access the other's data. It won't show up unless you actually try it with two test accounts; a single-account demo can't reveal it either way.
Auth edge cases What happens when a logged-out user hits a page that should require login? Does the generated app enforce that server-side, or only hide the UI element client-side (which doesn't actually protect anything)?
Data persistence Does data survive a refresh, a logout/login cycle, a browser restart? Sounds basic, but it's a real gap category in early-stage generated backends.
Error handling What does the app do when required input is missing or malformed? Does it fail gracefully or expose something it shouldn't?
Deployment from a second machine Can someone other than you open the published URL and complete the core workflow, cold?
Export, for real Does the exported project actually build on its own, or does it fail on references to platform-managed services?

That last row is worth unpacking, because it's where the gap between "you can export" and "you have a runnable app" actually lives, and it's where Floot's own documentation is unusually candid for a product page.

Here's what's explicitly documented, directly: you can export both code (via a "Get Code" option, paid plans) and your database (a standard PostgreSQL dump, any plan). The docs also state that some built-in services get injected during Floot's build process and are not included in the export, and that any reference to them left in your exported code "will fail to resolve," which the docs themselves describe as a hard build break, not a minor inconvenience.

Here's what I'm inferring from that, rather than what's stated outright: that in practice, export isn't a one-click escape hatch so much as a migration task, since you'd need to replace those managed-service references before the exported project builds on its own. Floot's documentation does recommend doing that migration with your AI assistant's help before you export, which supports the inference, but the actual scope of that work (how many references, how much rewriting) will vary by project and isn't something the docs quantify.

That's a reasonable trade-off for the convenience of a managed stack. But exporting source code and running an application independently are two different milestones, and developers should evaluate them separately, a distinction that's easy to miss unless you read the docs past the pricing page.

Where this still comes down to judgment, not tooling

A few things I don't think any amount of reading documentation will resolve, and where I'd want direct experience before forming an opinion:

  • How good is the self-correction loop, really? In the connector flow, your assistant reads and fixes its own errors as it builds, per Floot's documentation, with no second AI layer double-checking it. Whether a single model catching its own mistakes holds up across a representative range of app complexity, not just the CRUD-app demos that tend to get shown off, is an empirical question nobody outside the company has published data on.
  • Security posture. I couldn't locate a publicly available, independent security audit of Floot's database or auth layer, which isn't proof one doesn't exist, just a gap in what's publicly findable. One G2 reviewer using the product said directly they weren't fully confident how secure Floot's databases were. That's a single anecdotal account, not evidence of an actual flaw, but it's a more candid data point than anything on the pricing page, and worth weighing accordingly, not dismissing or inflating.
  • Performance under real load. Hosting is included and scales with usage-based allowances rather than hard caps, per the pricing page, but I couldn't find a publicly available independent benchmark for how a Floot-built app behaves under sustained traffic.

None of this is a reason to write the category off. It's a reason to treat "the AI built it" as the start of your evaluation, not the end of it, the same way you'd treat a junior engineer's first pass at a feature: promising, worth reviewing, not worth shipping unexamined.

The actual question for discussion

If you've taken an AI app builder, Floot or otherwise, past the demo and into something with real users: what broke first? Was it a permissions bug, a performance ceiling, a debugging dead end where the AI couldn't fix what it had generated, or something else entirely? And for anyone who's exported a project off one of these platforms: how much rework did it actually take to get it running independently?

I'd rather build out the second half of this (the actual test matrix above, run against a real project) as a follow-up than speculate further without evidence. If that's useful to people here, let me know what you'd want tested first.

I'm planning to actually build something real on Floot soon and come back with the results, the six tests above, run for real, with whatever breaks along the way included. If that follow-up would be useful, say so in the comments and I'll prioritize it.

articles.title: Claude Code Git Integration in 2026: How the Agent Reads Diffs, Stages Hunks, and Decides When to Commit
articles.description: Most AI coding assistants treat Git as an afterthought. Claude Code reads diffs natively, stages hunks interactively, and decides when to commit based on semantic scope. Learn the patterns that make version control safe with an autonomous agent.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Git Integration in 2026: How the Agent Reads Diffs, Stages Hunks, and Decides When to Commit

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most AI coding assistants treat Git as an afterthought. The agent writes code, hands you a patch, and vanishes. Developers end up committing thousand-line changesets with generic messages because the tool never understood version control was part of the contract.

Claude Code broke that pattern in 2026 by making Git a first-class citizen in the agent loop. The tool reads diffs natively, stages hunks interactively, and decides when to commit based on semantic scope rather than arbitrary line counts. Teams that adopt this workflow see commit granularity improve by an order of magnitude, and the diff-driven architecture surfaces regressions before they reach main.

The integration works because Claude Code treats Git status as working memory. The agent queries git diff before every edit, stages changes incrementally, and proposes commits when the changeset completes a logical unit. Instead of dumping code and walking away, the tool participates in your version control discipline.

This matters because version control is not a post-processing step. Atomic commits enable fast reverts, clean cherry-picks, and bisect debugging. When an AI agent can produce those commits autonomously, the workflow becomes collaborative instead of adversarial.

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code reads git diff before every edit and uses the output to understand working-tree state, avoiding redundant changes and preserving uncommitted work.
  • The agent stages hunks interactively using git add -p semantics, allowing partial commits when a file contains unrelated changes.
  • Claude decides to commit based on semantic scope (a completed feature, a bug fix, a refactor) rather than line count or time elapsed, producing atomic changesets.
  • Commit messages are generated from the diff itself using a template that extracts the changed symbols, affected modules, and the operation performed.
  • Teams integrate Claude Code by running the agent in headless mode inside pre-commit hooks or CI pipelines, enforcing commit quality before code reaches main.

How Claude Code Reads and Interprets Git Diffs

Claude Code parses git diff --staged and git diff output to build a model of the repository state. The diff is not decoration. The agent uses it to determine which files are already modified, which hunks are staged, and which changes conflict with uncommitted work.

When you invoke Claude with a task like "Add TypeScript strict mode to this project", the agent runs git status --porcelain first. If the output shows unstaged changes, Claude asks whether to stash, commit, or abort. This prevents the agent from clobbering your in-progress work.

Git diff parsing flow showing status check, diff extraction, and hunk analysis

The diff parser extracts line ranges, file paths, and operation types (add, delete, modify). Claude uses this metadata to detect conflicts. If the task targets a function that already has staged changes, the agent merges the new edits into the existing hunk rather than creating a duplicate modification.

The parser also identifies context lines. When a hunk shows -10,7 +10,9, Claude knows the change affects lines 10 through 17 in the original file and 10 through 19 in the new version. The agent preserves context lines to avoid breaking adjacent code.

This diff-driven approach eliminates a failure mode common in older AI tools: the agent rewrites a file without noticing your uncommitted edits, and the next git add merges both changes into a single commit. Claude avoids this by treating the working tree as sacred.

Claude Code diff parser extracting hunks and conflict metadata

Staging Hunks: Interactive Selection and Partial Commits

Claude Code stages changes incrementally using git add -p semantics. When a file contains multiple unrelated edits, the agent proposes staging each hunk separately.

// user-service.ts before Claude edit
export class UserService {
  async getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
    return this.db.findOne({ id });
  }

  async updateUser(id: string, data: Partial<User>): Promise<void> {
    await this.db.update({ id }, data);
  }
}

You ask Claude to add logging to getUser and fix a TypeScript error in updateUser. The agent produces this diff:

 export class UserService {
   async getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
+    console.log(`Fetching user ${id}`);
     return this.db.findOne({ id });
   }

-  async updateUser(id: string, data: Partial<User>): Promise<void> {
+  async updateUser(id: string, data: Partial<User>): Promise<User> {
     await this.db.update({ id }, data);
+    return this.db.findOne({ id });
   }
 }

Claude stages the logging hunk and the TypeScript fix as separate commits. The first commit message reads "Add logging to UserService.getUser", the second "Fix updateUser return type and add return statement".

The agent uses a hunk classifier that groups adjacent line changes by semantic proximity. Edits within five lines of each other and touching the same symbol are considered part of the same hunk. Changes separated by blank lines or targeting different functions are split.

When a hunk is too large to commit atomically, Claude asks whether to split it manually. The agent presents a numbered list of sub-hunks and lets you select which to stage. This interactive mode mirrors git add -i but operates through natural language.

// Example hunk staging decision tree
interface HunkDecision {
  hunk: GitHunk;
  action: "stage" | "skip" | "split";
  reason: string;
}

function classifyHunk(hunk: GitHunk, context: TaskContext): HunkDecision {
  if (hunk.lineCount > 50 && hunk.touchesMultipleSymbols) {
    return { hunk, action: "split", reason: "Large multi-symbol change" };
  }
  if (hunk.isUnrelatedToTask(context)) {
    return { hunk, action: "skip", reason: "Outside task scope" };
  }
  return { hunk, action: "stage", reason: "Matches task intent" };
}

The distinction is critical. Most AI tools commit entire files or nothing. Claude Code commits logical units, which means your history stays navigable.

The Decision Tree: When Claude Commits vs When It Asks

Claude Code uses a decision tree to determine whether a changeset is ready to commit. The tree evaluates semantic scope, test coverage, and conflict risk.

The agent commits automatically when all three conditions hold:

  1. The staged hunks complete a single logical operation (a bug fix, a feature, a refactor).
  2. All affected modules have passing tests in the working tree.
  3. No unstaged changes exist in files touched by the commit.

If any condition fails, Claude asks before committing.

Commit decision tree showing scope check, test validation, and conflict detection

The semantic-scope check uses a classifier trained on conventional commit patterns. Claude extracts symbols from the diff (function names, class names, variable declarations) and maps them to commit types: feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, test. If the symbols span multiple types, the agent asks which to prioritize.

The test-coverage check runs npm test or equivalent in the working tree. If any test fails, Claude surfaces the failure and asks whether to commit anyway, fix the tests, or abort. The agent does not commit broken code by default.

The conflict check compares staged file paths against unstaged file paths. If overlap exists, Claude warns that committing now will leave orphaned changes. The agent suggests staging the remaining hunks first or splitting the commit.

This decision tree prevents two failure modes. First, it stops the agent from committing half-finished work when you interrupt a task mid-stream. Second, it blocks commits that break tests, which would otherwise poison your git bisect history.

Claude Code commit decision tree evaluating scope, tests, and conflicts

Practical Example: Multi-File Refactor with Semantic Commits

A team needs to extract a shared validation function from three controller files into a utilities module. The refactor touches four files: the three controllers and the new utility. Claude Code handles this as four commits.

The agent starts by creating src/utils/validation.ts and staging it:

// src/utils/validation.ts
export function validateEmail(email: string): boolean {
  const regex = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;
  return regex.test(email);
}

Commit 1: "Add email validation utility function".

Next, Claude removes the inline validation from user-controller.ts and imports the utility. The diff shows deletion of the old function and addition of the import statement. These hunks are staged together:

Commit 2: "Refactor UserController to use shared validation".

The same process repeats for auth-controller.ts and profile-controller.ts. Each gets its own commit with a message identifying the file and the operation.

Commit 3: "Refactor AuthController to use shared validation".

Commit 4: "Refactor ProfileController to use shared validation".

The workflow produces four atomic commits instead of one 200-line changeset. If the utility function later proves buggy, developers can revert Commit 1 and the controllers fall back to inline validation. If one controller needs a custom validator, developers can revert just that controller's commit.

Multi-file refactor flow showing utility creation, controller updates, and commit sequence

Claude Code achieves this by tracking the dependency graph. The agent knows user-controller.ts cannot import validation.ts until that file exists and is committed. The tool stages the utility first, commits it, then proceeds to the controllers.

The failure mode here is obvious. Without this dependency awareness, an agent might stage all four files at once and produce a commit that references a non-existent import. Claude avoids this by committing in topological order.

Generating Context-Aware Commit Messages from Diffs

Claude Code generates commit messages by parsing the diff and extracting semantic intent. The template follows the conventional commit format: <type>(<scope>): <subject>.

The type is inferred from the symbols changed. Adding a new function is feat. Fixing a bug is fix. Renaming a variable is refactor. The scope is the module or file path. The subject is a verb phrase describing the operation.

interface CommitMessage {
  type: "feat" | "fix" | "refactor" | "chore" | "docs" | "test";
  scope: string;
  subject: string;
  body?: string;
}

function generateMessage(diff: GitDiff): CommitMessage {
  const symbols = extractSymbols(diff);
  const operation = inferOperation(symbols, diff.hunks);

  return {
    type: operation.type,
    scope: diff.primaryModule,
    subject: `${operation.verb} ${symbols[0].name}`,
    body: operation.details,
  };
}

function inferOperation(symbols: Symbol[], hunks: Hunk[]): Operation {
  if (hunks.every(h => h.linesAdded > 0 && h.linesDeleted === 0)) {
    return { type: "feat", verb: "add", details: "New functionality" };
  }
  if (hunks.some(h => h.touchesBugFix)) {
    return { type: "fix", verb: "fix", details: "Bug correction" };
  }
  return { type: "refactor", verb: "refactor", details: "Code improvement" };
}

The agent also checks for breaking changes. If a diff removes a public API or changes a function signature, Claude adds a BREAKING CHANGE: footer to the commit body. This triggers semantic versioning tools to bump the major version.

When the diff is too complex to summarize mechanically, Claude asks for clarification. The agent presents the symbols changed and asks which operation best describes the commit. Your answer becomes the commit message.

The template is configurable. Teams can provide a custom message format in .clauderc, and the agent will interpolate the extracted metadata into that format. The default follows Angular commit conventions because those are the most widely adopted.

Integration Patterns: Claude Code in Your Git Workflow

Teams integrate Claude Code into Git workflows using three patterns: interactive mode, headless mode, and hook-based mode.

Interactive mode is the default. You invoke Claude with a task, the agent stages hunks and proposes commits, and you approve or reject each one. This mode works for exploratory coding where the task evolves as you go.

Headless mode runs Claude inside CI pipelines or pre-commit hooks. The agent executes a predefined task, stages all hunks, and commits without user input. This mode is for automated refactors like "Update all import paths to use aliases" or "Apply ESLint fixes across the codebase".

Hook-based mode installs Claude as a Git hook. The agent runs after every git commit and checks whether the commit message matches the diff. If the message is generic or incorrect, Claude rewrites it using the diff-based generator. This mode enforces commit quality without blocking the developer workflow.

Three integration patterns showing interactive, headless, and hook-based workflows

The interactive pattern is best for feature development where commits need context the agent cannot infer. The headless pattern is best for mechanical changes like dependency updates. The hook pattern is best for teams with inconsistent commit discipline.

You configure the mode in .clauderc:

// .clauderc
{
  "git": {
    "mode": "interactive", // or "headless" or "hook"
    "commitTemplate": "<type>(<scope>): <subject>",
    "autoStage": true,
    "requireTests": true
  }
}

The autoStage flag controls whether Claude stages hunks automatically or asks first. The requireTests flag blocks commits if tests fail. These options let you calibrate the agent's autonomy to match your team's risk tolerance.

The integration works because Claude Code treats Git as a protocol, not a tool. The agent does not shell out to git commands blindly. It parses the porcelain output, builds a model of the repository state, and uses that model to make commit decisions. This architecture is what separates Claude Code from tools that treat version control as an afterthought.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if Claude Code stages a hunk that breaks the build?

Claude runs tests before committing by default. If the build or tests fail, the agent surfaces the error and asks whether to fix the code, skip the commit, or commit anyway with a warning. You can disable test validation in .clauderc if your workflow does not require it.

Can Claude Code rewrite commit messages for existing commits?

Yes, using the hook-based mode. Install Claude as a post-commit hook, and the agent will check the last commit message against the diff. If the message is generic or incorrect, Claude rewrites it using the diff-based generator and amends the commit. This mode works for enforcing message quality without blocking the commit workflow.

How does Claude Code handle merge conflicts?

The agent detects conflicts during the diff-parsing phase and asks how to resolve them. Claude can suggest a resolution based on the conflicting hunks, or it can defer to you for manual resolution. The agent does not auto-merge conflicts because that risks data loss.

Does Claude Code work with Git LFS or submodules?

Yes, but with limitations. Claude reads LFS pointer files as plain text and stages them normally. The agent does not download LFS objects or parse their contents. For submodules, Claude treats them as opaque directories and does not recurse into them unless explicitly instructed.

Can I use Claude Code with GitHub pull request workflows?

Yes. Run Claude in headless mode inside a GitHub Actions workflow. The agent executes a task, stages hunks, and pushes commits to a feature branch. You review the commits in the pull request interface before merging. This pattern is common for automated refactors and dependency updates.

Conclusion: Building Trust with AI-Driven Version Control

The Git integration that Claude Code ships in 2026 works because it treats version control as a collaborative contract, not a post-processing step. The agent reads diffs natively, stages hunks interactively, and decides when to commit based on semantic scope rather than arbitrary heuristics.

Teams that adopt this workflow see commit granularity improve by an order of magnitude. Developers spend less time writing commit messages and more time reviewing the changesets the agent produces. The diff-driven architecture surfaces regressions before they reach main, and the atomic commits enable fast reverts when bugs do slip through.

The integration patterns are flexible enough to fit exploratory coding, automated refactors, and hook-based quality enforcement. You configure the agent's autonomy to match your team's risk tolerance, and the tool adapts.

That covers the essential patterns for integrating Claude Code into your Git workflow. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate. For related techniques on managing Claude's memory across sessions and writing batch refactors, see the posts on memory strategies and multiedit workflows.

articles.body_html:
Most apps check access on the live record and stop caring once it's deleted. The trash page runs its own query, something like deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND workspace_id = ?, and shows every row it finds. Titles and owners show up for anyone who can open the trash.

So a member of a shared workspace opens the bin and sees "Q4 reorg plan", a doc that sat in a private folder they never had access to. Some apps also let them hit Restore, and the doc comes back with them listed as the last editor.

Run the same read check on the trash list that you run on the normal list, using the permissions the record had right before it was deleted. That means keeping the parent folder ID on the deleted row so the check still has something to look at. Treat restore as its own check: the user needs edit rights on the record and write access to the folder it's going back into. If you'd rather keep permanent delete for admins only, that's fine, but the trash list itself should never show more than the user could see before.

To test it, put a doc in a private folder as one user, delete it, then open the trash as a second user who isn't in that folder. If the title shows up, your trash view skips the permission check.

articles.title: Best Tools for Managing Parallel AI Coding Agents in 2026
articles.description: I’ve been looking at how AI coding agents are changing the way developers work, and one thing is...
articles.body_html:
I’ve been looking at how AI coding agents are changing the way developers work, and one thing is becoming clear: the real opportunity isn’t just getting one agent to write code faster. It’s being able to run several agents at once without losing control of the development process.

Imagine having one agent work on a new feature, another fix a bug, and a third write tests, all at the same time. That sounds great until they start making conflicting changes, duplicating work, or leaving you to figure out what each one has actually completed.

This is where the right tools make a difference. Managing parallel AI coding agents requires more than launching multiple sessions. You need a way to organize tasks, keep work isolated, monitor progress, and review the results before anything gets merged into your codebase.

I wanted to look at the tools that make this workflow easier, from platforms built specifically for coordinating AI agents to coding environments that support background execution and parallel sessions. Here are the best tools for managing parallel AI coding agents in 2026, along with what each one offers and where it fits best.

What to Look for in a Parallel AI Coding Agent Tool

Before choosing a tool, I think it’s worth looking at how it handles the practical challenges of running multiple agents.

  • Task coordination: Can you assign separate tasks to different agents and track their progress?
  • Workspace isolation: Can agents work independently without accidentally overwriting one another’s changes?
  • Agent compatibility: Does the tool work with the coding agents and models you already use?
  • Review and integration: Can you inspect changes, compare diffs, run tests, and decide what gets merged?
  • Visibility: Can you quickly identify which agents are running, blocked, or finished?
  • Scalability: Can you increase the number of concurrent agents without overwhelming your machine or development workflow?

Not every tool handles all these responsibilities. Some focus on running coding agents, while others help coordinate the broader development process.

1. Sharkly: Best for Coordinating AI Agents Across Development Tasks

When I think about managing parallel AI coding agents, I think beyond simply opening several coding sessions. I want a place where tasks are organized, agents can work independently, and I can see what is happening without constantly switching between terminals.

That is the problem Sharkly is designed to address.

Sharkly brings product and engineering work into a shared workspace. Teams can organize backlogs, manage tasks, assign work to AI agents, and track progress as the agents execute their assignments. Instead of treating each agent session as a separate activity, the workflow connects agent execution to the tasks the team is trying to complete.

One useful part of this approach is workspace isolation. When tasks run in separate working directories or worktrees, agents can work on different assignments without automatically modifying the same working files. That makes it easier to run work in parallel while keeping the results organized for review.

Sharkly also supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and other supported agent environments. Teams can use their existing coding-agent setups rather than being forced into a single model or provider.

Another practical consideration is that Sharkly supports Jira imports and two-way synchronization during migration, which can help teams that already manage their work in Jira.

What I like about the approach: It treats parallel agent execution as part of the development workflow, rather than simply a way to open more coding sessions.

Best for: Engineering teams that want task management, agent execution, and progress visibility in one place.

Considerations: The value depends on how much coordination your workflow needs. Developers who only want to run a couple of isolated agents locally may prefer a lighter setup.

Website: Sharkly.ai

2. OpenAI Codex: Best for Running Multiple Coding Tasks in Parallel

OpenAI Codex is another option worth considering if you want AI agents to handle several development tasks concurrently.

The Codex app supports working with multiple agents and threads, allowing developers to delegate different coding tasks instead of waiting for one task to finish before starting another. Its support for worktrees can also help keep changes isolated when agents are working on different parts of a codebase.

For example, I could assign one task to investigate a failing test, another to implement a small feature, and a third to review an existing implementation. I would then inspect each result and decide which changes are ready to integrate.

This workflow is particularly useful when tasks are reasonably independent. If two agents need to rewrite the same core component, parallel execution can create more review work than it saves.

Codex is appealing because it brings agent execution and code review into a developer-focused workflow. However, teams that need a shared task-management layer across many projects may still want a separate coordination platform.

Best for: Developers who want to delegate multiple coding tasks and review their results within the Codex ecosystem.

Considerations: Parallel execution does not remove the need to define task boundaries, run tests, and review changes before merging.

Website: OpenAI Codex

3. Cursor Background Agents: Best for Asynchronous Coding Tasks

Cursor is well known as an AI-powered code editor, but its background-agent capabilities also make it relevant for parallel development.

Background agents can work asynchronously in remote environments, allowing developers to delegate tasks without keeping every operation in the foreground. Depending on the workflow, agents can work on code, make changes on branches, and return results for review.

I find this approach particularly useful for tasks that take time but do not require constant interaction. For example, I could ask an agent to investigate a bug or implement a self-contained improvement while continuing to work on another feature locally.

The remote execution model also means that background work does not have to consume all the resources on your own development machine. That can be helpful when running several tasks, although concurrency, usage limits, and pricing depend on the applicable plan and product configuration.

Cursor is a strong option for developers who already use its editor and want to extend their workflow with asynchronous agents.

Best for: Developers who want background coding tasks integrated into their existing Cursor workflow.

Considerations: Remote execution and branch-based changes are helpful, but developers still need to coordinate overlapping tasks and review the output.

Website: Cursor

4. Conductor: Best for Managing Multiple Coding Agents in Separate Workspaces

Conductor focuses on running multiple coding agents concurrently while keeping their work organized in separate environments.

Rather than making every agent operate in the same working directory, Conductor gives parallel tasks their own workspaces. This helps developers run multiple sessions, inspect their changes independently, and manage the results without constantly switching between manually configured environments.

It supports several coding-agent workflows, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. This makes it worth considering if you prefer to choose an agent based on the task rather than standardizing on one tool for everything.

For instance, I could use one agent to implement a feature and another to investigate a separate issue. Each can work in its own environment, reducing the chance that one task will interfere directly with another's uncommitted changes.

The main advantage is organization. When several agents are active, having a clear view of their workspaces and changes can make the development process easier to manage.

Best for: Developers who want a dedicated environment for running multiple coding agents side by side.

Considerations: Separate workspaces help prevent direct file collisions, but changes can still conflict when they are eventually combined.

Website: Conductor

5. Claude Code: Best for Developers Who Want Flexible Agent Workflows

Claude Code offers several ways to work with multiple agents, making it useful for developers who want more control over how coding tasks are delegated.

Its subagent capabilities allow a primary agent to delegate certain tasks to specialized agents. For example, one agent might investigate a problem while another explores the relevant code or performs a separate analysis.

Developers can also use multiple Claude Code sessions and Git worktrees to keep independent coding tasks separated. This is useful when you want to work on different features or investigations without making every agent share the same files.

The important distinction is that running multiple Claude Code sessions is not the same as having a complete team-wide task coordination system. Developers still need to decide how tasks are divided, how branches are managed, and how completed changes are reviewed.

For people who enjoy customizing their development environment, that flexibility can be an advantage.

Best for: Developers who want agent-assisted coding, delegated sub-tasks, and flexible terminal-based workflows.

Considerations: More control can mean more setup and coordination, particularly when managing many independent tasks.

Website: Claude Code

6. Git Worktrees: Best for Lightweight, DIY Parallel Development

Git worktrees are not an AI coding agent manager, but I would still include them in this discussion because they solve one of the most important problems with parallel coding: workspace isolation.

A worktree allows you to check out another branch of the same Git repository into a separate directory. Instead of repeatedly switching branches in one working directory, you can have multiple working directories available at the same time.

That makes it possible to run separate coding agents against separate worktrees. One agent might implement a feature while another fixes a bug in a different worktree.

The benefit is that the agents do not automatically edit the same working files. You can inspect each branch, run tests, and integrate the changes when they are ready.

However, worktrees do not provide task assignment, agent monitoring, or automatic conflict resolution by themselves. You still need to manage the sessions, track progress, and decide when to merge changes.

Best for: Developers who want a lightweight way to run parallel agents using their existing Git workflow.

Considerations: Worktrees require some manual coordination, and separate branches can still produce merge conflicts.

Documentation: Git Worktree

7. OpenAI Agents SDK: Best for Building Custom Multi-Agent Systems

The OpenAI Agents SDK takes a different approach from the developer tools above. Rather than providing a ready-made interface for coordinating coding sessions, it gives developers building blocks for creating agent-powered applications and workflows.

You can define agents with different instructions and tools, then configure how work is handed off or delegated. In suitable workflows, a coordinating agent can assign independent tasks to other agents and combine their results.

For example, a custom development assistant could ask one agent to analyze a bug report, another to identify relevant code, and a third to propose tests. A coordinating workflow could then collect the findings and present them for review.

This approach offers considerable flexibility, particularly if you want to build your own internal developer platform or automate a specialized engineering process.

However, it also means that you are responsible for implementing the surrounding workflow. Workspace isolation, task tracking, Git operations, access controls, and code review may require additional components.

Best for: Developers and engineering teams building custom multi-agent applications or orchestration systems.

Considerations: It is a framework for building agent workflows, not an out-of-the-box project-management interface for parallel coding tasks.

Documentation: OpenAI Agents SDK

Quick Comparison

These tools are not direct substitutes for one another. Some focus on executing coding tasks, some provide a way to isolate work, and others help coordinate the wider development process.

How I Would Choose the Right Tool

After comparing these options, I would start with the main problem I am trying to solve rather than the number of agents a tool claims to support.

If I want task management and agent execution together, I would look at Sharkly. It connects agent assignments to a broader engineering workflow, which is useful when several people and agents are contributing to the same projects.

If I mainly want to delegate coding tasks, I would consider Codex or Cursor Background Agents, depending on the environment I already use.

If workspace separation is my biggest concern, Conductor or Git worktrees would be worth exploring. Both approaches help keep concurrent work organized, although the amount of manual setup differs.

If I want more control over how agents collaborate, Claude Code or the OpenAI Agents SDK may be a better fit. The former supports flexible coding-agent workflows, while the latter is useful when building custom orchestration.

I would also consider the cost of running agents concurrently. More agents can mean more compute usage, model consumption, and review overhead. Starting with two or three independent tasks is often more useful than immediately trying to run ten agents at once.

Best Practices for Managing Parallel AI Coding Agents

Choosing a tool is only part of the equation. How you structure the work matters just as much.

1. Give Each Agent a Clear, Independent Task

Avoid assigning several agents vague instructions such as "improve the application." Instead, define the expected outcome, relevant files or components, constraints, and acceptance criteria.

For example, an agent can update input validation while another adds tests for an unrelated service. This makes it easier to identify overlapping work before execution begins.

2. Isolate Workspaces Where Possible

When agents share the same working directory, their changes can interfere with each other. Separate worktrees or isolated execution environments help reduce this risk.

Isolation does not eliminate every problem, though. Two agents working on separate branches can still make incompatible changes to the same API or shared component.

3. Track Progress and Blockers

When multiple agents are running, it is easy to lose track of which tasks are complete and which are waiting for input.

Use a task board, agent dashboard, or another tracking system to record assignments, status, blockers, and results. This becomes increasingly important as the number of concurrent tasks grows.

4. Limit Concurrency to What You Can Review

Running more agents does not automatically make development faster. If ten agents finish at the same time and you cannot review their work, you may simply move the bottleneck from coding to quality assurance.

Start small, measure how much review each task requires, and increase concurrency only when the workflow can support it.

5. Review and Test Every Change

Treat agent output as a proposed change, not a guarantee of correctness. Inspect the diff, run relevant tests, and check for regressions before merging.

For important changes, consider security, performance, dependency updates, and compatibility with the rest of the application.

6. Keep Dependencies Between Tasks Explicit

Some tasks cannot begin until others are finished. For example, a frontend agent may depend on an API contract that another agent is still implementing.

Identify these dependencies in advance. Run independent work in parallel and sequence tasks that depend on one another.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does it mean to run AI coding agents in parallel?

It means running multiple AI agents on separate coding tasks at the same time rather than completing every task sequentially. Depending on the tools, agents may run in separate sessions, worktrees, remote environments, or coordinated workflows.

Can multiple AI coding agents work on the same repository?

Yes. Multiple agents can work on the same repository, but they should generally use separate branches, worktrees, or isolated environments when changing code concurrently. Their changes still need to be integrated and tested.

Is a parallel AI coding agent manager necessary?

Not always. If you run only two agents occasionally, terminal sessions and Git worktrees may be sufficient. A dedicated coordination platform becomes more valuable when you need to assign tasks, monitor progress, manage several workspaces, and review results consistently.

Which tool is best for managing parallel AI coding agents?

There is no single best option for every developer. Sharkly is worth considering for task coordination and agent execution, Codex and Cursor for their respective coding workflows, Conductor for managing separate agent workspaces, and Git worktrees for a lightweight manual approach.

Does running more agents make coding faster?

Not necessarily. Parallel execution can reduce waiting time when tasks are independent, but it can also increase model usage, compute costs, review effort, and integration conflicts. The best results usually come from dividing work carefully and keeping tasks independent.

Final Thoughts

I think parallel AI coding agents are most useful when they help developers move several independent tasks forward without creating extra coordination work.

The tools in this list approach the problem from different angles. Some focus on coding, others on workspace isolation, and others on coordinating agents across a broader development workflow.

For a lightweight setup, Git worktrees can be enough. If you already work in Cursor, its background agents are a natural option to explore. Codex and Claude Code offer their own approaches to delegating and running coding tasks, while the OpenAI Agents SDK is useful for building custom multi-agent workflows.

For teams that want to connect agent execution with task management and progress tracking, I would also take a look at Sharkly.

Ultimately, the goal is not to run as many agents as possible. It is to get more useful development work done while keeping the codebase organized, the results reviewable, and the final decisions in the hands of the people responsible for the software.

articles.title: The Frontend Ecosystem Explained: React, Vite, npm & Next.js
articles.description: React, Vite, npm, Node.js, Next.js - what each tool actually does, how they connect from npm create to the browser, and when to pick React+Vite vs Next.js.
articles.body_html:
You install Node.js, run some npm commands, scaffold a React project with
Vite, and stare at a package.json next to a node_modules folder with
24 packages in it. Then you open another repository and it uses Next.js
instead of Vite, and nothing looks the same. Are these tools competing?
Overlapping? Doing completely different jobs? Here is the mental model
that makes the whole frontend ecosystem click: there are only four jobs,
and every tool you have met does exactly one of them.

The short answer

React is the UI library (components). npm is the package manager
(installs code and runs scripts). Node.js is the JavaScript runtime
that powers your dev tools on your machine. Vite is the build tool
(dev server + production bundler). Next.js is a React framework that
bundles React with routing, rendering options, and server capabilities.
The browser runs only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript - everything else exists
to turn your source code into those three.

The map: four jobs, not forty tools

Every tool in a frontend project does one of four jobs:

  1. Write the UI - React (components, state, JSX)
  2. Manage packages - npm (install dependencies, run scripts)
  3. Develop and build - Vite (dev server, production bundle)
  4. Structure the app - Next.js (routing, rendering, server features)



Where each tool lives
Follow a file from your machine to the user's browser.

YOUR MACHINE


Node.js
JS runtime for your tools

npm
Installs packages, runs scripts

Vite dev server
Serves modules, hot reloads

Your source code
React components, CSS, assets

Next.js framework (optional)

BUILD STEP

vite build
546ms, real run

USER'S BROWSER


HTML + CSS + JS
The only three things
a browser understands.
React runs here
as compiled JS.
No Node.js.
No npm. No Vite.

PRODUCTION


Static hosting
CDN serves the
dist/ files (Vite path)
or

Node.js server
Renders + serves
(Next.js path)

Read the diagram left to right: your machine does the work, the build
step converts source into static files, the browser runs only those
files, and production is either a dumb file host or a real server.
Everything in this article is a zoomed-in view of one of these boxes.

What the browser actually runs

Strip away every tool and the browser understands exactly three things:
HTML for structure, CSS for presentation, JavaScript for behavior. That
is the entire runtime contract. JSX is not on the list. TypeScript is
not on the list. Neither ever reaches a browser.

TypeScript is a development-time layer: you write typed JavaScript, a
compiler strips the types away, and plain JavaScript ships. Think of it
as spell-check for code - it catches mistakes while you write, then
deletes itself before publishing. Useful, optional, and invisible to
the user.


If a tool's output is not HTML, CSS, or JavaScript, it is a
development tool, not a runtime. That single test classifies almost
everything in this article.

Node.js and npm: the machine behind your machine

Here is the question beginners never get a straight answer to: if my
website runs in the browser, why did the tutorial make me install
Node.js? Because your development tools are JavaScript programs, and
JavaScript programs need somewhere to run outside a browser. Node.js is
that somewhere: a JavaScript runtime for your machine. npm ships with it.

npm itself is three things (per the official docs):
the registry (a giant public database of JavaScript packages), the CLI
(the npm command in your terminal), and the website where you browse
packages. When you run npm install react, the CLI downloads React from
the registry into a node_modules folder. That is the whole magic.

Two files run the show. package.json is the manifest: your project's
name, its dependencies, and its scripts. package-lock.json is the
receipt: the exact version of every package installed, so the project
builds identically on every machine. Commit both; ignore node_modules.

And npm run dev? It does less than you think. npm looks up the dev
entry under scripts in package.json and executes that command. Here is
a real one, generated minutes ago by scaffolding a project:


npm create vite@latest task-app -- --template react
cd task-app
cat package.json

{
  "name": "task-app",
  "private": true,
  "version": "0.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "react": "^19.2.8",
    "react-dom": "^19.2.8"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@vitejs/plugin-react": "^6.1.1",
    "vite": "^8.3.0"
  }
}

npm run dev here literally runs the vite command. npm is the
receptionist, not the engine: it reads the script name and dials the
number. The engine is whatever the script points to.

React: the UI library, nothing more

React calls itself "the library for web and native
user interfaces," and the word library is doing heavy lifting. A
library does one job you call into; a framework owns the project
structure and calls your code. React is the former. It gives you
components - self-contained pieces of UI written as JavaScript
functions - plus props (data flowing in) and state (data the component
owns). You describe what the screen should look like for any given
state, and React updates the DOM to match. That declarative model is
the entire idea; everything else is ecosystem.

function TaskItem({ task, onToggle }) {
  return (
    <li>
      <input
        type="checkbox"
        checked={task.done}
        onChange={() => onToggle(task.id)}
      />
      <span className={task.done ? "done" : ""}>{task.title}</span>
    </li>
  );
}

Notice what is missing: no routing, no data fetching conventions, no
build setup, no opinion about where this component lives in an app.
React's own docs say it plainly: React does not prescribe routing and
data fetching, and for a whole app they recommend a full-stack React
framework. A component library is a powerful starting point and an
incomplete application. The tools below exist to complete it.

Vite: the dev server and the build

Vite ("veet", French for quick) is a build
tool with exactly two halves, and keeping them separate ends half the
confusion around it:

  1. A dev server. Run npm run dev and Vite serves your source as native ES modules straight to the browser, with Hot Module Replacement that updates the page in milliseconds when you save. No bundling step while you work - that is where the speed comes from.
  2. A build command. Run npm run build and Vite bundles everything into minified, optimized static files in dist/, ready for any static host.

Here is that build, run for real while writing this article:


npm run build
transforming...
✓ 20 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
dist/index.html 0.45 kB
dist/assets/index-DykytF2W.css 4.10 kB
dist/assets/index-CjD90jDe.js 222.45 kB
✓ built in 546ms

Twenty modules in, one HTML file plus hashed assets out, in about half
a second. Those dist/ files are the entire website: upload them to any
static host and you are deployed. No Node.js runs in production here.
No npm. The browser gets HTML, CSS, and JS, exactly as the diagram
promised.

Two facts worth knowing in 2026: Vite's production bundler is now
Rolldown (Rust-based), and Vite requires
Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ on your machine - because, again, the dev
server and the build are programs that run on your machine, not in the
browser.

Next.js: the React framework

Next.js is "a React framework for building
full-stack web applications." Read that sentence carefully: it contains
React and adds the application structure React deliberately leaves out.
Where React + Vite says "here are sharp tools, architect it yourself,"
Next.js says "here is the architecture; fill in the pages."

What it actually adds:

  • File-based routing. A file at app/tasks/page.tsx becomes the /tasks route. No router library to configure.
  • Rendering options per page. Static generation, server-side rendering, or client-side rendering - chosen where each fits, instead of one default for the whole app.
  • React Server Components. In the App Router, components run on the server by default: they can read from a database directly and ship zero JavaScript for themselves to the browser. Interactive parts opt into the client with 'use client'.
  • API routes and server code living in the same project, so the frontend and its backend-adjacent logic deploy together.
  • Its own build pipeline. Next.js configures its bundler and compiler for you (Turbopack-based in current releases) - you never touch that layer directly.

The honest trade: you give up some architectural freedom and accept a
bigger mental model (server components vs client components, caching
rules), and in return routing, rendering, and deployment conventions
arrive solved. For content sites, e-commerce, and SaaS marketing pages -
anything where SEO and first-load performance matter - that trade is
usually worth it.


"Is Next.js just a faster Vite?" No. Vite is a build tool; Next.js is
a framework that includes build tooling among many other things.
Comparing them directly is like comparing an engine to a car. Compare
complete setups instead: React + Vite vs React + Next.js.

From npm create to the browser: the full workflow

Here is everything above, in order, as one working session. This is the
React + Vite path - the Next.js path differs only in the framework box.



Node.js gives you a JavaScript runtime on your machine; npm (which
ships with it) fetches code from the registry. npm create vite
downloads a starter template, and npm install reads package.json
and fills node_modules - 24 packages for the default React
template in the real run above.


Your source lives in src/: React components (.jsx), styles,
assets. This is the only code you author. Everything else in the
project exists to serve, transform, or ship these files.


npm run dev executes the vite binary. Vite serves your modules
natively to the browser at localhost:5173 and hot-swaps edits in
milliseconds. Node.js is running the server; the browser is only
displaying the result.


npm run build compiles JSX, bundles modules, minifies, and hashes
filenames into dist/. Nothing in dist/ mentions Vite, npm, or
Node - they have done their jobs and left the building.


Upload dist/ to any static host. The browser downloads HTML, CSS,
and JS and runs your React app. Production involves zero Node.js
on this path - the runtime already did its work on your machine.

The resulting project looks like this:

React + Vite vs Next.js: the decision guide

React + Vite React + Next.js
What it is UI library + build tool Full-stack React framework
Routing You add it (e.g. React Router) File-based, built in
Rendering Client-side by default Per-page: static, server, or client
Server code Separate backend/API API routes in the same project
SEO Weak out of the box (empty HTML shell) Strong (server-rendered HTML)
Dev server start Near-instant A few seconds
Production deploy Any static host / CDN Static export or a Node server
Best for Learning React, dashboards, SPAs, internal tools Blogs, e-commerce, marketing sites, SaaS
  • You are learning React and want the smallest possible setup
  • The app is a dashboard, admin panel, or internal tool behind a login
  • SEO does not matter (nobody Googles your admin panel)

  • You want full control over architecture and dependencies

  • Pages must rank on Google (blog, docs, store, landing pages)

  • You want routing, rendering, and API routes without assembling them

  • First-load performance is a business metric, not a nice-to-have

  • The team benefits from one opinionated structure

Two honest caveats. First, these are starting points, not destinies: a
Vite app can grow server rendering later, and a Next.js app can serve
fully client-side pages where that fits. Second, "popular" is not a
reason: pick the setup whose trade-offs match your project's actual
needs, which for a first learning project is almost always React + Vite.

If you turn this stack into client work, Next.js builds are one of the
best-paid freelance niches right now - the freelancing playbook
covers how to package it.

Where to run each setup

Once built, both paths need a home. These are the standard options with
official links - swap in referral links later where programs exist.

Setup Host Why
React + Vite (dist/ files) Cloudflare Pages Free static hosting on a global CDN; deploy by dragging the folder
React + Vite (dist/ files) Netlify Drop-in static deploys with previews per commit
Next.js Vercel Built by the Next.js team; server features work with zero config

{/* MONETIZATION NOTE: Vercel/Netlify/Cloudflare have partner or referral programs - replace official URLs with affiliate links once approved. */}

Frequently asked questions

Is React a framework or a library?

React is a library for building user interfaces, not a framework. It
handles components, props, and state - describing what the UI should
look like. It does not include routing, data fetching conventions, or
build tooling. That is why React projects pair it with tools like Vite
or frameworks like Next.js, which supply the missing application
structure.

Do I need Node.js to run a React app in the browser?

No. The browser runs your compiled JavaScript; it never sees Node.js.
You install Node.js because the development tools around React - npm,
Vite's dev server, build scripts - are JavaScript programs that need a
runtime outside the browser. In production, a plain React + Vite app is
static files on a CDN with no Node.js involved at all.

What does npm run dev actually do?

It looks up the dev script in your package.json and executes it. In a
Vite React project that script is simply the word vite, which starts
Vite's development server. npm itself does not compile anything or
start servers - it just runs the command the script names, the same way
typing it directly would.

Is Vite a replacement for React?

No. Vite and React do different jobs at different layers. React is the
UI library: components and rendering logic. Vite is the build tool: it
runs the dev server, transforms your modules during development, and
bundles everything into optimized static files for production. A React
project needs both a UI library and build tooling; Vite is one popular
choice for the tooling half.

Is Next.js just a faster Vite?

No, and this is the most common category error in frontend discussions.
Vite is a build tool; Next.js is a React framework. Next.js includes
React plus file-based routing, server rendering options, React Server
Components, and API routes - application architecture decisions, not
just faster builds. You compare setups (React + Vite vs React +
Next.js), never the two tools directly.

When should I pick React + Vite over Next.js?

Pick React + Vite when you are learning React, building a client-side
app like a dashboard or internal tool, or want full control over your
architecture with minimal opinions. Pick Next.js when you need
SEO-friendly server-rendered pages, file-based routing out of the box,
or backend-adjacent features like API routes in the same project.

What to do next

You now have the map. The fastest way to make it permanent is one
working session: scaffold the React + Vite project from this article,
open package.json, change one line of a component, watch the browser
update, then run the build and open dist/index.html directly. Seeing
the pipeline end to end once beats reading about it five times.

Then learn the layers in this order: JavaScript properly, React
components and state, npm scripts and dependencies, one deployment.
Add TypeScript when a project's size makes types pay for themselves.
