articles.title: I built a site chatbot that isn't allowed to make things up
articles.description: In 2024 a tribunal in Canada made Air Canada honor what its website chatbot had told a customer about...
articles.body_html:
In 2024 a tribunal in Canada made Air Canada honor what its website chatbot had told a customer about refunds. The airline argued the bot was responsible for its own words. The tribunal said the company is responsible for everything on its site, chatbot included.

For a small business that is the real problem with site chatbots. A wrong opening time or an invented price costs more than the bot saves. So I built a demo where the model is only allowed to draft, and plain code decides what the customer sees: Front Desk.

The setup

The demo runs on Juniper Street Bakery, a bakery I made up. Its whole "site" is 13 short entries: hours, prices, cakes, allergens, delivery, payment. The assistant knows nothing else.

The model is Gemma 4 E2B, running in the browser through WebLLM at temperature 0. Every question goes through four steps:

  1. Find. Code picks up to three entries that match the question. If nothing matches, the model is not asked at all and the customer gets the phone number.
  2. Draft. The model reads only those entries and returns JSON: the answer, the id of the entry it used, and the sentence it took the answer from.
  3. Check. The quoted sentence has to be in that entry. Every number in the answer has to be in it too ("4 pm" counts as 16:00, "$4" does not count as $4.50). And every word that carries meaning has to appear somewhere in what the model was given.
  4. Show or step back. If the first sentence fails a check, the draft is thrown away and the customer sees the entry's exact text or the contact details. Later sentences that fail are cut.

What the first runs showed

I wrote 24 test questions with known answers, 6 of them about things the site never mentions (pizza, a loyalty card, Christmas hours).

Run 1: 17 of 24. No invented fact reached the customer, but most misses had the same cause. Asked "Do you deliver bread?", the model set answerable: false, because to it "no" felt like "not answerable". Rewording that rule fixed it.

Run 2: 21 of 24, and a real hole. Asked "Do you have a loyalty card?", it answered "No, we do not have a loyalty card." The site says nothing about loyalty cards. There were no numbers in that sentence, so my number check let it through.

That is where the word check came from: "loyalty" is not in anything the model was given, so the sentence is not backed by the site. The same check later cut "That is our capacity." from an otherwise correct answer about seats.

On questions I hadn't tuned on

After writing the checks I added 7 new questions and ran all 31 live. It got 28 right, 5 of the 7 new ones. One miss was my own bug: the model wrote "$8.00" and the site says "$8", and the number check treated them as different. With that fixed, the same recorded drafts pass 29 of 31.

The two misses left are worth showing, because the checks can't catch them:

  • "Is the bakery open on Christmas Day?" got the regular opening hours. True, every word on the site, but not an answer.
  • "Is the cinnamon roll vegan?" got a correct "no", but pointed at the pastry prices instead of the vegan entry.

A wrong yes or no where every word is on the site would pass the same way. That is why I think a bot like this needs a test set of the business's real questions before it goes live, not only a good prompt.

Do small businesses even have chatbots?

I took 1,020 business websites in Austin from OpenStreetMap (cafes, restaurants, dentists, clinics, salons, bakeries), dropped chains that share one domain, and fetched each homepage once. 592 loaded. 27 had any chat widget at all. 15 of those were Wix's built-in chat with the owner. The only ones I could identify as AI assistants were on chain sites.

So the chatbot market is crowded, but the local cafe mostly has no assistant at all.

A widget without a model

That led to a second mode. The widget is one script tag. Without a model endpoint it runs in quote mode: it finds the entry that matches and shows it word for word, or gives the phone number. It cannot make anything up and costs nothing per question. On the 31 test questions it shows the right entry or declines 29 times, though I also used those questions while choosing search words, so expect less on a new site.

With an endpoint added, it drafts answers and runs the same checks, falling back to quote mode when one fails.

Try it

  • Demo with recorded answers, no download: https://phazww.github.io/front-desk/#recorded
  • Live model and the test set: https://phazww.github.io/front-desk/#tests (needs WebGPU, downloads the model once)
  • Code: https://github.com/phazww/front-desk

I set this up for small businesses on their own content, with a test set of their customers' questions. Cafes and bakeries first: https://phazww.github.io/front-desk/cafes/

What would you check that I'm not checking?

articles.title: Free Online Image Tools Are Not Free. Here Are the Receipts.
articles.description: Description: Resolution caps, "we delete it after 2 hours (trust us)", paywalled buttons, and why...
articles.body_html:
Description: Resolution caps, "we delete it after 2 hours (trust us)", paywalled buttons, and why your browser can now do all of this by itself.

You know the ritual.

You need one transparent PNG of a product photo. Five minutes, tops. You google
"remove background online", click the first result, upload, and watch the progress bar
do its little dance.

The preview? Gorgeous. Clean edges. You hit download.

And you get a postage stamp. 🖼️

Let's talk about why "free online image tools" is mostly a vibe, not a price tag, and
about the genuinely interesting engineering reason this whole category is overdue for a
rewrite.

🧾 Receipts policy: every limit I quote below comes from the tool's own
documentation or pricing page. No hot takes without sources.

💀 Sin #1: The bait-and-downscale

remove.bg is the poster child, and to their credit they say it out loud in their
own FAQ: the free website version is for low-resolution images, up to 0.25 megapixels.
Full resolution (up to 50 MP) lives behind premium plans and credits.

Do the math with me:

0.25 MP  =  250,000 pixels  ≈  625 × 400

A modern phone photo is 12 MP. That's roughly 48× more pixels than what the
free tier hands back. The preview on screen looks sharp because your screen is small.
The file is where the shrinkage happens.

Fair play: servers cost money, GPUs cost more, and freemium is a legit business
model. But "free" and "free at thumbnail size" are not the same product.

🕵️ Sin #2: Your photos go on a little vacation

Here's the thing most people never think about. For the typical online tool, the
architecture is:

 your photo ──HTTPS──▶ their server ──▶ (processing) ──▶ their server ──▶ you
                         ▲
                 a copy exists here.
                 for "a while".

Take iLoveIMG: the files go to their servers, and they say uploads get deleted
within about two hours. That's a reasonable policy, honestly. But notice what it
actually is: a promise, not a property of the system. You can't verify it. You're
trusting a privacy page.

For a meme? Whatever. For an ID scan, a client's unreleased product shots, your
kid's school photo, a screenshot with a token in it? That's a bigger ask than the
"drag & drop" button makes it look like.

🔒 Sin #3: Paywall roulette

You open Canva, find the Background Remover button right there in the Edit panel,
click it, and get the upgrade prompt. The feature is a Canva Pro thing. You get a
limited free taste, and then it's subscription time.

Again, not evil, just the pattern: the button is free to look at.

🧱 Sin #4: Limits that hit exactly when you need it

TinyPNG is a great compressor and I will defend that. But the free web version
tops out at 20 images per session, 5 MB per image, and 3 conversions. Paid
tiers raise that to 75 MB (Pro) and 150 MB (Ultra).

RAW-ish export from a camera? A big screenshot? Over 5 MB, no entry. 🚪

🔁 Sin #5 (the one nobody counts): the Tab Spiral

Real task: "Make this product photo web-ready, transparent, under 200 KB, as WebP."

Real workflow with single-purpose tools:

Site A  remove background   → upload #1 → download
Site B  resize              → upload #2 → download
Site C  compress            → upload #3 → download
Site D  convert to WebP     → upload #4 → download

That's 4 uploads, 4 privacy policies, 4 free-tier limits, and 3 extra lossy
re-encodes (every JPEG save throws away a bit more detail; it's called generation
loss). You didn't edit an image. You ran a relay race with your pixels. 🏃

🤔 So why does it work like this?

Historically: the browser couldn't do the heavy part. Segmentation models needed
GPUs and big runtimes, so the model lived on a server, and your photo had to travel
to it. Server costs → limits → upsell → "download HD for 1 credit."

That excuse has been quietly expiring for a few years:

Then Now
JS is too slow for ML WebAssembly runs near-native code in the tab
No runtime for neural nets ONNX Runtime Web runs real models in-browser
Models are 500 MB+ Good segmentation/inpainting models ship in the 5 – 180 MB range
Can't cache big files Cache Storage keeps a model after the first download

Meaning the "server" in the diagram above is now… optional:

 your photo ──▶ [ your browser tab: WASM + model ] ──▶ you
                         ▲
                 nothing leaves.
                 there is no "their server" step.

Don't trust me. Verify it. 🔍

Any tool that claims "100% client-side" should survive this 20-second test:

  1. Open DevTools → Network tab.
  2. Clear it. Load an image and run the tool.
  3. Look for any request that carries your image bytes.

A real on-device tool shows no image upload. (You'll see one-time downloads of the
model files, because the AI has to come from somewhere, but those flow to you,
not from you.) Try this on whatever you use today. It's genuinely eye-opening.

Credit where due: Squoosh (from the Chrome team) has been proving in-browser
image work is viable for years. The tech is not exotic anymore. It's just that
nobody bundled the whole workflow in one place.

🧪 The nerdy bit: why most cutouts look "off" (even the AI ones)

This is the part I find fun, and it's where "just run a model" stops being enough.

Problem A: the mask is tiny

Segmentation models run at a fixed size, commonly around 1024×1024 (lightweight
ones: 320×320). Your photo is bigger. On a 4032×3024 shot, one pixel of the mask
covers roughly a 4×3 block of real pixels.

Stretch that mask up naively and you get the classic crime scene: soft, blobby edges,
hair turned into a helmet. 🪖

Fix: use the photo itself as a guide. A guided filter (He et al.) snaps the
blurry mask onto the real edges in the full-res image:

// idea in one breath:
// alpha  = upsample(modelMask)                // blurry but in the right place
// guide  = luminance(photo)                   // sharp, knows where edges really are
// alpha' = guidedFilter(guide, alpha, r, eps) // edges now follow the photo
// then clamp alpha' to a narrow band around the model's own edge
// so it can sharpen the boundary, but never invent or delete regions

Problem B: the halo 🌈

Edge pixels are a mix of subject and old background. Cut the subject out of a green
screen-ish photo and drop it on white: green fringe. Every time.

Fix: estimate the true foreground colour at edge pixels (Blur-Fusion foreground
estimation, Forte & Pitié) and use that instead of the contaminated original. Interior
pixels stay byte-for-byte original; only the fringe gets repaired.

Problem C: memory is the real boss fight 💣

A 12 MP RGBA buffer is 48 MB. (12,000,000 × 4 bytes.) Now count how many full-size
copies a naive "remove object" pipeline makes: source, mask, blurred mask, model
output, blend buffer... phones start sweating at ~500 MB and then the OS just ends
your tab.

Fix: never process the whole photo. Crop the region around what you're editing
(plus context), run the model on that, blend it back, and leave every other pixel
untouched.

whole-photo pipeline:  cost ∝ size of the photo   → 💥 on phones
region pipeline:       cost ∝ size of the edit    → ✅ boring, which is the goal

Good engineering is making the scary thing boring.

😅 Okay, disclosure time

Everything above is the checklist I kept running into, until I got annoyed enough to
build against it. I'm the dev behind APIC Web,
a browser-based image toolkit, so yes, this is where I tell you about it. But you've
read this far, so let me at least be straight about what it is and isn't.

What it is: everything in the "Tab Spiral" in a single tab.

Tool What it does
✂️ Remove Background On-device AI cut-out (IS-Net from the DIS research; Light/Fast/Max tiers), guided-filter edge refinement + colour-fringe removal, keeps your original resolution
🧽 Remove Object Paint over it, AI fills it in (MI-GAN, Picsart research, MIT-licensed); only the region around your brush is processed
📐 Resize Clean multi-step downscaling
🔄 Convert PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF
🗜️ Compress Type a target size in KB; it binary-searches the highest quality that fits
🎛️ Edit + Advanced Filters, light/colour controls, crop, undo/redo

Your image is processed in your browser, and the Network-tab test above is the
proof, not my word.

The honest tradeoffs (because you'd find them in 5 minutes anyway)

  • 🔑 Sign-in: the tool panels sit behind a free Google sign-in. Guests can I store account basics (name, email), never your images.
  • ⬇️ First-run download: the AI models download once (~5 MB Light, 44 MB Fast, 176 MB Max for Remove BG; ~28 MB for Remove Object) from a public model host, then get cached in your browser.
  • 📱 Phones play by phone rules: weaker devices default to the lightweight model, and huge photos (above roughly 12 MP) get downsized on phones only, specifically so the tab doesn't crash. Desktop is never capped.
  • 🧠 It's not Photoshop. No layers, no templates, no brand kits. It's built for the 90% of "I just need this one image fixed" moments.

The scorecard

Typical free tool APIC Web
Free output resolution often capped original resolution
Where your photo goes uploaded to a server stays in your tab
Verify it yourself? trust the privacy page Network tab
Background removal paywall / credits included
Workflow 4 sites, 4 uploads one tab
Re-encodes along the way many one export

🚀 Try to break it

I'd rather you roast it than ignore it:

👉 akhouri-anmol-kumar.github.io/APIC-web

Throw your worst photo at it: messy hair, a glass bottle, a low-contrast product,
a 12 MP phone pic on a potato Android. Open the Network tab while you do it. If it
fails, tell me in the comments (the phone-crash fix I mentioned came straight
from user complaints, so I take them seriously).

And if you've got your own "free tool betrayed me" story, drop it below. I'm
collecting them. 👇

articles.title: AI-generated content gets cited more than human content in Google AI Overviews. That should bother you." published: false
articles.description: A peer-reviewed paper published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (volume 318, Canadian...
articles.body_html:
A peer-reviewed paper published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (volume 318, Canadian Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2026) found something that should make anyone producing content for the web uncomfortable:

AI-generated documents are cited more frequently than human-authored documents in Google AI Overviews, even after controlling for retrieval rank.

The study, by Rustem Kakimov, Xing Tan, Jonathan Gillham, and Narcis Bejtic, proposed a framework for auditing citation behavior in AI-generated search summaries. They applied it to Google AI Overviews on "Your Money or Your Life" queries drawn from the MS MARCO Web Search dataset, which covers topics where accuracy matters most: health, finance, and safety.

What they found

The key finding, quoted from the abstract:

"AI-generated documents are cited more frequently than human-authored documents even after controlling for retrieval rank, with the difference driven primarily by non-retrieved citations and most pronounced at highly ranked positions."

Three things to notice in that sentence:

  1. "Even after controlling for retrieval rank" means this is not a side effect of AI content ranking higher. At the same rank position, AI-generated content gets cited more often than human content.
  2. "Driven primarily by non-retrieved citations" means the AI is pulling in AI-generated content through a path that does not go through normal retrieval. It is finding AI content that does not appear in the organic results and citing it anyway.
  3. "Most pronounced at highly ranked positions" means the bias toward AI content is strongest at the top, where citations matter most for visibility.

Why this happens

The paper does not prove a causal mechanism, but the pattern is consistent with what we know about how LLMs process text. Language models generate text by predicting the most likely next token. When they evaluate which source to cite, they are doing something similar: measuring which passage best fits the response being generated. AI-generated text, which is itself the product of likelihood maximization, tends to match the model's own output patterns more closely than human text does.

A commenter on Hacker News put it plainly: "I can consistently reproduce this by asking Claude which code snippet it prefers: the one it generated in a different chat, or one that I refactored for my own needs and find more useful. It always picks its own."

This is not a bug. It is a structural property of how generative retrieval works. The system that generates the answer also selects the sources, and it has a preference for text that looks like what it would produce.

The Google angle

Google's official AI optimization guide says: "If an AI can write your article on its own, it will never cite you." The guide frames this as advice: produce content that AI cannot generate, and you will be cited.

The Kakimov study suggests the inverse is also true: content that AI can generate is more likely to be cited, because the retrieval system prefers text that matches its own output distribution. The two statements are not contradictory. They describe the same phenomenon from two sides: non-commodity human content gets cited because it is unique, and AI-generated content gets cited because it matches the model's preferences.

The uncomfortable middle is where most content lives: human-written but indistinguishable from what AI would produce. That content gets cited less than both extremes.

What this means for content strategy

The implication is not "use AI to write your content so it gets cited more." That would accelerate a feedback loop where AI generates content, AI retrieves it, and AI cites it, with human voices pushed to the margins.

The implication is that the content most likely to be cited by AI search engines falls into two categories:

Content that AI cannot produce. Original research, first-hand experience, proprietary data, expert analysis with a specific point of view. Google's guide calls this "non-commodity content." The Kakimov study confirms it gets cited because it adds something the model does not already have.

Content that AI produces. AI-generated summaries, listicles, and generic informational content. These get cited because they match the model's output patterns, but they are also the content most likely to be replaced by the AI generating its own response without citing anyone.

The danger zone is the middle. Well-optimized, well-structured, accurate human content that covers the same ground an AI would cover. It is too generic to be "non-commodity" and too human to match the model's preferences. It gets cited less than both extremes.

The feedback loop problem

If AI-generated content is cited more, and citations drive traffic and authority, then AI-generated content accumulates more authority signals over time. Those authority signals feed back into ranking and retrieval. The system rewards the content it produces.

This is the same pattern that Google's own guide warns against when it says "if AI can write your article, it will not cite you." But the Kakimov data suggests the warning is incomplete. AI can and does cite AI-generated content, at rates higher than human content, in the most sensitive query categories.

The researchers highlight "the importance of transparent, measurement-based auditing for understanding citation behavior in generative search systems." They are right. The only way to know whether this bias is growing, stable, or correcting is to measure it continuously. Right now, almost no one is.

What I am doing about it

The audit tool I maintain, geo-optimizer-skill, does not score content on whether it is AI-generated. Detecting AI content reliably is an arms race, and any heuristic I ship will be outdated within months.

What it does instead is score content on specificity signals: original data, first-hand language, specific examples, and citation-worthy passages. Content that scores high on these signals tends to be non-commodity regardless of who wrote it. Content that scores low tends to be the generic informational text that falls into the danger zone.

That is the practical filter. Not "is this AI-generated" but "does this contain something the retrieval system cannot generate on its own." If the answer is yes, it gets cited. If the answer is no, the data says it gets cited less than both the AI content and the original human content, and the gap may be widening.

articles.title: The One-Line Package That Broke create-react-app
articles.description: A tiny npm library shipped a "minor" release and broke some of the biggest JavaScript tools for three hours. What it teaches every backend engineer about Semantic Versioning.
articles.body_html:
Minor Release, Major Damage

Here is the entire job of a package called is-promise:

function isPromise(obj) {
  return !!obj && (typeof obj === 'object' || typeof obj === 'function')
    && typeof obj.then === 'function';
}

One function. It checks whether something looks like a Promise.

That's it.

In April 2020, it was being downloaded around 12 million times a week. GitHub counted about 3.5 million projects depending on it, mostly without knowing it existed.

On Saturday, 25 April 2020, its maintainer published version 2.2.0.

Within hours, people trying to start a new project with create-react-app, angular-cli or firebase-tools were staring at an error instead.

The version number said minor. Nothing about the result was minor.

What the Version Number Promised

Semantic Versioning gives every release three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

  • PATCH means a bug fix. Nothing new, nothing removed.
  • MINOR means something new was added, and everything that worked before still works.
  • MAJOR means something changed in a way that can break you. Read the notes before upgrading.

That promise is what makes automatic upgrades possible. When a project lists a dependency as "is-promise": "^2.1.0", the caret says: give me any 2.x version from 2.1.0 upward. Patches and minors flow in on their own, because SemVer says they're safe.

Python works the same way. requests~=2.31 or django>=5.0,<6.0 in your requirements are the same bet: anything below the next MAJOR shouldn't break you.

So when 2.2.0 appeared, thousands of dependency trees picked it up with nobody clicking anything.

That's the system working exactly as designed. It's also why a mislabelled release spreads so fast.

What Actually Changed

Version 2.2.0 was the first release of is-promise in about five years. The maintainer, Forbes Lindesay, wanted to modernise it: add support for ES Modules, JavaScript's newer import system, while keeping the old CommonJS require() working.

The changes were small and reasonable:

  • A default export, so modern code could import isPromise from 'is-promise'.
  • An exports field in package.json, the newer way of telling Node which file to load for which module system.
  • Updated TypeScript definitions.

To the author, this was an addition. New way to import it, old way still there. That's the textbook definition of MINOR.

The problem was one line in package.json. The exports field pointed to "index.js" instead of the format Node expects, a path starting with ./. Node rejected it outright:

Error [ERR_INVALID_PACKAGE_TARGET]: Invalid "exports" main target "index.js"
defined in the package config
  • It only failed on newer Node. Versions from 12.16 onward had started reading the exports field by default. Older Node ignored it, which is probably why it worked on the author's machine.
  • Lockfiles didn't save anyone. Many reports came from people running npx create-react-app. Tools run through npx install fresh, and a library's lockfile isn't used when someone else installs it. Every new project got 2.2.0.
  • One tiny package sat deep in big trees. Nobody chose is-promise. It came in through a dependency of a dependency.

The maintainer moved fast. Around three hours later, version 2.2.2 was out, and it simply dropped the ES Module support. The modern version eventually shipped properly, as a new MAJOR release: 4.0.0.

The Question That Would Have Caught It

Here's the detail I find most interesting.

Node's own documentation on dual-module packages already said that adding exports and type to an existing package is a breaking change. Even when done perfectly, the exports field changes which files consumers are allowed to load. Anyone who imported a deep path like is-promise/index.js could break even with a correct config.

So the honest version number was 3.0.0, before the typo was even made.

The author labelled the release by intent: I'm adding a feature. SemVer asks about impact: what will your users notice?

Those are different questions, and they give different answers more often than we admit.

The question I use now, for libraries and for APIs, is:

"Can anyone using this observe the difference?"

Not "did I mean to break something." Not "is this technically a feature." Just whether someone on the other side could notice.

The Same Trap in Your Backend

You don't need to publish npm packages to fall into this. Every backend API has consumers, and the same gap between intent and impact shows up in ordinary tickets:

  • Tightening validation. You add a minimum length on a username field. It feels like an addition. But a request that returned 200 yesterday returns 400 today. You removed something.
  • Fixing a value. Your API returned status labels in the wrong language, and you fix it. Any client that matched on the old strings now breaks. With enough users, someone depends on every observable behaviour, bugs included. That idea even has a name: Hyrum's Law.
  • Correcting a calculation. Same field, same type, different number. If clients make decisions on it, their decisions just changed without warning.
  • Adding a field. Usually safe. Not for clients with strict schema validation that rejects unknown fields.

Here's the decision tree I'd put in a pull request template:

Can any consumer observe the difference?
│
├── NO  → PATCH (internal fixes, performance, logging)
│
└── YES → What kind of difference?
          ├── Removes, renames, or changes a type        → MAJOR
          ├── Rejects input that used to be accepted     → MAJOR
          ├── Changes how the package/API is loaded      → MAJOR
          ├── Changes the meaning of an existing output  → MAJOR, or MINOR with advance notice
          └── Adds something optional                    → MINOR

The is-promise change sits on the third branch. It changed how the package was loaded, which is exactly why it needed a new MAJOR.

When a Patch Really Is a Patch

None of this means every release should be MAJOR.

A slow query made faster is a patch. An internal log nobody else can see is a patch. A crash fixed in a code path that never returned anything useful is a patch.

And inflating versions has its own cost. If every release is "breaking," consumers stop reading the number and pin everything forever. Then they miss your security fixes too.

The version only works as a signal if it's honest in both directions.

"It's only a small change" isn't evidence. "It works on my machine" definitely isn't.

What the Maintainer Did Next

The best part of this story is how it was handled.

Forbes Lindesay shipped a fix within hours and wrote a public post-mortem. He added end-to-end tests that install the package the way a real user would, then check it actually loads. And the ES Module support came back later as a proper major version instead of a minor.

It was an honest mistake that could have happened to almost anyone. What's worth copying is the response: test from the consumer's side, and let the version number tell the truth.

The Real Lesson

Semantic Versioning looks like it's about code. It's really a promise to the people who depend on you, written in three numbers.

is-promise didn't break because it was small, or because one-line packages are silly. It broke because the version described what the author meant to do, while millions of installs depended on what the release actually did.

Before you pick the next version number, ask one question:

"Can anyone tell the difference?"

If they can, the PATCH or MINOR has to justify itself.

Your turn 👇

What's the smallest release you've seen break something big? I'd like to hear the gray-zone stories other engineers have run into. Share yours in the comments.

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

How This Started

I've been doing a little research on how good AI models are with uncommon, niche languages. And Georgian, my native language, is my main test subject. Check out the article for more details:

Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules
Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission
Giorgi Kobaidze
Giorgi Kobaidze
Oct 11

Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules

#devchallenge #kagglechallenge #ai #machinelearning
68 reactions Comments 34 comments
20 min read

While comparing outputs, I kept noticing that the hardest parts weren't vocabulary. They were structure: things Georgian simply doesn't encode that English requires, and the other way around.

And because I'm a developer, my brain immediately filed these under one label: language features. Some features make life easier, some make it harder, and almost all of them are trade-offs.

I'll compare English and Georgian, since those are the only two languages I know (for now, German is in progress). I love both of them, and both are beautiful in their own way. But they couldn't be more different. Georgian has its own alphabet, Mkhedruli, with 33 letters and no uppercase or lowercase in everyday writing. Yes, my native language is case-insensitive by design. We don't really need casing at all.

Let's look at two features.

Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them)

English marks whether a noun is definite (a specific thing the listener already knows about) or indefinite (something new or non-specific). That's the whole job of the versus a/an.

I saw a bus leaving the station. The bus was a white MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and a Greyhound badge on it.

Georgian has no articles at all. Structurally, the same sentence looks like this:

I saw bus leaving station. Bus was white 1999 MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and Greyhound badge on it.

In actual Georgian:

დავინახე, როგორ გადიოდა ავტობუსი სადგურიდან. ავტობუსი იყო თეთრი MCI 102-DL3, ვერცხლისფერი დისკებით და Greyhound-ის ემბლემით.

No articles. None. Zero. Null. Undefined.
The listener figures out definiteness from context: what was mentioned before, word order, and the situation itself. The first "bus" is obviously new information, the second one is obviously the same bus.

That doesn't mean Georgian is helpless when it needs precision. It just reaches for other tools on demand:

  • Demonstratives like ეს (this) and ის (that) make something definite:

this/that bus

  • In casual speech, ერთი (one) often works like an indefinite article:

ერთი კაცი შემხვდა ("I met a (certain) man")

The Upside

It's simpler. Fewer words to say and write, and nothing to choose. You never have to stop and think about which article goes where, which is famously one of the hardest parts of English for people whose native languages don't have articles.

The Downside

It's not explicit, and implicit things occasionally become ambiguous. Rarely, but it happens. If someone tells you:

Take bus

Do they mean a bus, any bus, or the bus that's standing right in front of you? In real life, the speaker resolves it with intonation, a gesture, or by saying:

Take this bus

But that doesn't always happen.

And here's where it connects back to my AI research: when a model translates Georgian into English, it has to insert information that wasn't in the source. Every "a" and "the" in the output is a guess. Usually a good one, but still a guess.

Feature #2: Gender

From what I've observed, languages are absolutely obsessed with sorting things by gender. But there are actually two different things going on, and it's worth separating them:

  • Natural gender: pronouns reflect the actual gender of a person. That's English.
  • Grammatical gender: every noun belongs to a class, including spoons, tables, and the moon. That's Italian, German, and many others.

English: He, She, and It

English has he/him/his, she/her/hers, and it/its. That's as far as it goes, and it mostly follows reality: people get he or she, a table is "it". (Except ships, which are sometimes "she" for reasons sailors would have to explain.)

Italian: Two Genders, Every Noun

Italian has masculine and feminine, and every noun has to pick one. There are patterns (nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, -a usually feminine), and then the exceptions show up:

  • la mano (hand) is feminine, despite ending in -o
  • il problema (problem) is masculine, despite ending in -a
  • il sole (sun) is masculine, la luna (moon) is feminine

Logic behind it? Nobody knows. Well, at least I don't. You just memorize them.

German: Three Genders

Think that's complex? German has three: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). Look at your dinner table:

  • der Löffel: the spoon is masculine
  • die Gabel: the fork is feminine
  • das Messer: the knife is neuter

Three pieces of cutlery, three genders. It gets better: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter, because the diminutive suffix -chen always makes a word neuter. Grammar beats biology. And the sun and moon? die Sonne is feminine and der Mond is masculine, the exact opposite of Italian. If gender were logical, the two languages would at least agree on the sky.

I recently started learning German, and honestly, der/die/das is the hardest part for me. The standard advice is to never learn a noun without its article, and now I understand why.

Georgian: Zero Genders

When I was a kid and started learning other languages, this was the weirdest thing of all. Why on earth are words divided by gender? That was absolute nonsense to me. Because in Georgian, there's no gender. None. Zero. Not even for people.

The same pronoun covers he, she, and it: ის (he/she/it), მას (him/her/it, as an object), მისი (his/her/its). The only distinction Georgian makes is between people and things, with ვინ (who) versus რა (what). Which is natural. Nobody asks:

Who is that truck?

The Upside of Gender

It carries information.

My boss is really lovely, she told me I'm doing a great job during the meeting.

One pronoun, and you already know your boss is a woman.

It helps you track references. This is the advantage people rarely mention. In German:

Die Gabel liegt neben dem Löffel. Sie ist schmutzig.

Sie can only be the fork, because the fork is feminine and the spoon isn't. In English, the same sentence is ambiguous:

The fork is next to the spoon. It is dirty.

In Georgian, it's equally ambiguous. Grammatical gender works like a checksum: redundant information that helps the listener connect the right pronoun to the right noun.

The Downside of Gender

What if you don't know?

Tell your boss to give you some vacation days, he or she should be concerned that you're working so much.

Now you have to say both, and it gets clunky fast.

English's escape hatch is singular "they":

When a developer joins the meeting, ask them to show you where the repository is.

One developer, plural pronoun. My first instinct was that this is technically incorrect, but it turns out English speakers have been doing it since the 14th century, and writers like Shakespeare and Jane Austen used it. Even better: English has done this exact trick before. You was originally plural only; the singular was thou. Over time, "you" took over the singular too, and nobody today thinks "you are" is a grammar bug. Singular "they" is the same migration, still in progress.

The memorization tax. For people, gender carries meaning. For spoons and forks, it carries none, yet Italian and German learners still have to memorize it for every single noun.

The Downside of Having No Gender

Georgian's simplicity has a price too. If you want to express gender, you have to say it explicitly: man or woman, gentleman or lady. "My friend" (მეგობარი) tells you nothing about who that friend is.

And once again, this is a real problem for AI. Translating ის into English forces a choice between "he" and "she" that the original sentence never made. Machine translation systems have historically filled that gap with stereotypes: the doctor becomes "he", the nurse becomes "she". Those assumptions are never good.

Complexity Doesn't Disappear, It Moves

Before anyone concludes that Georgian is "easy mode", it isn't. Far from it, it's so complex, sometimes even native speakers struggle to speak or write grammatically correct, It just stores its complexity somewhere else, mostly in verbs.

A single Georgian verb can encode both the subject and the object. მიყვარხარ means "I love you". One word, three ideas. Verbs change form across groups of tenses, and even the case of the subject changes depending on the tense. Georgian dropped articles and gender, then poured all that saved effort into verbs that do an enormous amount of work.

There's a principle in software for exactly this: Tesler's law, or the law of conservation of complexity. Complexity can't be removed, only moved. Languages, it seems, follow it too.

Sounds Familiar, Developers?

All of this reminded me of programming languages, because they face the exact same trade-offs.

Articles vs. var

Georgian's missing articles map almost perfectly onto type inference in C#:

Bus bus = new Bus("MCI 102-DL3");   // explicit: "the bus"
var bus = new Bus("MCI 102-DL3");   // implied, but obvious from context
var next = dispatcher.Next();        // ...is that a Bus? A Route? "take bus"

The compiler always knows what next is. The human reading the code might not. That's why many teams have a style rule along the lines of "use var only when the type is obvious from the right-hand side". It's the Georgian rule exactly: implicit is great when the context makes it obvious, and when it doesn't, you say "this bus" or write the type out.

C# even went in the other direction with target-typed new, where the left side carries the information and the right side drops it:

Bus bus = new("MCI 102-DL3");

Same idea, different side of the sentence.

Gender vs. Typing

German grammatical gender behaves a lot like static typing. Every noun carries a tag, and everything around it (the article, the adjective endings) has to agree with that tag. It's ceremony, and sometimes it feels like noise, but mismatches get caught and references are easier to track.

Georgian pronouns are closer to dynamic typing. ის can hold anything: a person, a truck, an idea. Less ceremony, more flexibility, and meaning gets resolved at "runtime" from context.

C# won't let you mix types without saying so:

int distance = 5;
string label = "2";
var total = distance - label;
// error CS0019: Operator '-' cannot be applied to operands of type 'int' and 'string'

JavaScript will happily guess what you meant:

"5" - 2   // 3
"5" + 2   // "52"
[] + []   // ""

(To be precise, static vs. dynamic and strong vs. weak are two different axes. Python is dynamic but strongly typed: "5" + 2 raises a TypeError. JavaScript is dynamic and weakly typed, which is how you get "52".)

And the arbitrary part of German gender? Imagine a language that forces you to annotate every variable with a type, where the type names were assigned by rolling dice centuries ago, and nobody is allowed to refactor. That's der Löffel, die Gabel, and das Messer.

Languages That Evolve (and Ones That Mostly Don't)

Here's where natural languages and programming languages really differ.

Programming languages learn from each other constantly. C# is a great example. It added generics, then lambdas and LINQ (borrowed from the functional programming world), pattern matching inspired by F# and the ML family, records, and nullable reference types to fight what Tony Hoare called his "billion-dollar mistake". And it doesn't only borrow, it lends: async/await, introduced in C# 5, was later adopted by JavaScript, Python, Rust, and many others.

Natural languages mostly borrow words. English took beef, pork, and mutton from French after the Norman conquest, while the living animals stayed cow, pig, and sheep. Georgian borrowed კომპიუტერი (computer) and ტელეფონი (telephone) like nearly every other language on Earth. Sometimes a borrowed word wins so completely that people forget the original word in their own language ever existed.

The structure, on the other hand, usually stays put. Usually. Natural languages do refactor, just very slowly:

  • Old English had three grammatical genders, just like German. By the Middle English period, they were gone. English deprecated a feature that German still ships today.
  • Thou was deprecated, and you absorbed its job, which is exactly the precedent for singular "they".

The difference is the release process. There's no changelog and no migration guide, a breaking change takes a few centuries to roll out, and every speaker is a maintainer.

Every Language Is a Trade-Off

No matter what design you come up with, there will always be trade-offs. Articles buy precision and cost effort. Gender buys information and reference tracking, and costs memorization. Dropping both buys simplicity and costs explicitness, then the complexity sneaks back in through the verbs.

Every language is beautiful in its own right, and the same goes for programming languages. Learning a new one, spoken or compiled, is the best way to discover assumptions you didn't even know you had. Georgian taught me that a language can live perfectly well without "a/an/the" and "she/he". C# taught me why var needs a style guide. And German is currently teaching me how insanely hard it is.

As for AI: the places where languages disagree on what to encode are exactly the places where models have to guess. Which is precisely why I'm benchmarking them in Georgian.

Tell Me About Your Language

Now it's your turn. What languages do you speak, and how do they handle these features? Do they have articles? Grammatical gender? Is your native language "statically" or "dynamically" typed? Tell me in the comments. I'd love to see which languages follow the same patterns and which break all the rules.

articles.title: What Are Your Chances of Surviving Resident Evil Based on Your Tech Job?
articles.description: I recently watched the new Resident Evil movie. 🎬  Watching the main character stumble from one...
articles.body_html:
I recently watched the new Resident Evil movie. 🎬

Watching the main character stumble from one disaster into another was absurdly funny and a little heartbreaking. But what impressed me most was his professional commitment. He is a courier, and no matter what happens around him, he never forgets the job: the package must reach its destination.

I will avoid major spoilers here. You can join this discussion even if you have not seen the movie.

But I have to say this first: the main character deserves real credit for his work ethic. He is not a trained superhero. He is an ordinary courier who takes “deliver at all costs” to its absolute limit. That level of professional commitment is genuinely admirable.

So this thought experiment is not making fun of his decision. It uses his commitment as the starting condition:

You are just as dedicated to your profession as he is to delivering that package.

You cannot resign, call in sick, close the ticket, or simply refuse the mission. You still have to do your job and move forward. Your only advantage is the way your profession has trained you to think.

This is not a serious disaster survival guide. It is just a fun career question inspired by a horror movie. 😄

The city is failing. The ticket is still open.

Then I started wondering: what if I were in his place?

I have worked in QA for 15 years. If I carried all those testing habits into an extreme situation, what would my survival rate be?

My answer is: 50%. 🎲

Not because I can fight monsters. I cannot.

My advantage is that a QA engineer rarely trusts a happy path just because somebody says it should work.

QA Might Try to Stop the Story Before It Starts 🧪

Imagine receiving this task:

Deliver the only copy of a critical item into a city that is clearly falling apart. The environment is unknown. The recipient may be offline. There is no backup route.

My first questions would be:

  • Who created this requirement?
  • Is the recipient still online?
  • Why is there only one copy of the critical item?
  • Where is the backup?
  • What is the rollback plan?
  • Why are we continuing the happy path when production is already throwing alerts everywhere?

Without the “you must be as dedicated as the protagonist” rule, the movie might end in ten minutes. I would return the ticket with this comment:

Preconditions are incomplete. The recipient is unreachable. The production environment is unstable. Release blocked.

Unfortunately, our rules say I still have to continue.

This is where testing experience might help. One strange event can be random. Two might require investigation. But when the roads, people, communications, and infrastructure all fail at the same time, a senior QA should recognize a systemic failure.

The answer is not to keep following the original route. Pause that path. Isolate the risk. Find a safer alternative. Then continue the mission.

Why Testing Skills Might Improve My Odds

I would not casually bring a strangely behaving person into my only vehicle.

That would be the survival equivalent of connecting unvalidated, high-risk input directly to the only production environment that still works.

Before entering an unfamiliar building, I would also check:

  • Where is the exit?
  • Is there a second route?
  • Can the door be opened from the inside?
  • What happens if the power fails?
  • Is this plan dependent on a single point of failure?

I would not assume that something is permanently dead just because it fell over once. I would also avoid putting all hope into one sample, one laboratory, one vehicle, or one person.

Fifteen years in QA has taught me at least one thing:

Every critical process without a backup is just waiting for a sufficiently unlucky day.

That is why I give myself a 50% chance.

Testing experience might help me spot danger earlier, challenge bad assumptions, and stop a broken flow. But it cannot solve fitness, luck, limited resources, or unknown biological monsters.

Fifty-fifty is already my optimistic estimate.

QA Could Also Die From QA Habits 🐛

Of course, being a tester does not automatically make someone good at survival.

Our greatest risk is the need to reproduce a bug.

I might escape safely, then suddenly stop and think:

What exactly triggered that mutation? Distance? Time? Sound? Temperature?

Then I would go back to collect logs, record a better video, and attempt a second reproduction.

Or I might reach the exit, notice one unopened door, and say:

The main flow passed. I will test one last edge case before I leave.

At that moment, my survival probability drops from 50% to 5%. 🚨

The most dangerous sentence in QA: “One last edge case.”

What About Your Tech Job? 🧑‍💻

The same rule applies to you. You bring the same admirable professional commitment that the courier brings to his delivery. You cannot end the story by saying, “Not my ticket.” You must keep doing your job while using your professional skills to stay alive.

Every tech role has a possible survival advantage and a potentially fatal professional habit.

Frontend Engineer

They quickly notice that none of the exits provide useful status feedback and the city map violates every basic UX principle.

Unfortunately, they may spend valuable time complaining that the emergency door has no hover state.

Backend Engineer

They try to identify the source of the infection chain and shut down the upstream service.

They may also believe that restarting the core system will somehow fix everything.

DevOps / SRE

They check monitoring, capacity, failover, and backup regions. They would never trust a cure deployed as a single instance.

However, while every alarm in the city is firing, they might still be deciding whether this is a real incident or a broken alert rule.

Security Engineer

They trust nobody, no attachment, and no unknown device. Their isolation instincts may be the strongest of any profession.

They may also enter the most dangerous area just to prove the full impact of a vulnerability.

Data Engineer

They build a model from infection times, locations, and behavior patterns.

First, they must accept that half the data is missing, every source uses a different format, and there is no schema documentation.

Product Manager

They ask for the goal, target user, priority, and success metric before the outbreak begins.

Then, during the evacuation, they ask whether we can add multiplayer collaboration to the MVP.

AI / Agent Engineer

They send one agent to scout ahead and another agent to review the first agent's conclusion.

The biggest risk is that both agents confidently report “Task completed successfully” while the critical package is still sitting where it started.

Your Turn 🎯

Give yourself a survival probability based on your real profession.

You can use this format in the comments:

Role:
Years of experience:
Survival probability:
My biggest professional advantage:
The professional habit most likely to get me killed:
My first survival rule:

Here is mine:

Role: QA / Test Engineer
Years of experience: 15
Survival probability: 50%
My biggest professional advantage: I do not ignore repeated anomalies or trust a single happy path
The professional habit most likely to get me killed: Going back to reproduce the bug one more time
My first survival rule: When every monitor is alerting, pause the main flow, isolate the risk, and roll back

In the ideal ending, I survive the night, preserve the logs, reproduce every critical issue, and submit this bug report:

Severity: Critical
Reproduction rate: 100%
Impact: Entire city
Recommendation: Block the release immediately

The next morning, Umbrella management replies:

Status: Rejected
Reason: Known issue. No fix planned. Does not affect core business.

Known issue. No fix planned. Apparently production can continue.

Again, this is a silly thought experiment, not an actual survival guide. 😂

And every percentage comes with one final condition: do not run into a Tyrant, Nemesis, or any of the franchise's main characters. If you are a random civilian standing next to the protagonists, your survival rate is basically zero. 😂

Now it is your turn:

If you were dropped into Resident Evil and had to rely on your professional skills, what would your survival probability be—and why?

articles.title: AI-Generated Tests Can Agree With the Bug
articles.description: When an AI agent writes both the implementation and its tests, a green build may only prove that the same wrong assumption was encoded twice.
articles.body_html:
An AI coding agent implements a feature, generates tests, runs them, and opens a pull request with a green build.

That looks like independent verification. It often is not.

If the implementation and the tests came from the same prompt, repository context, and interpretation of the requirement, they can repeat the same mistake. The code is wrong. The tests confidently prove that the wrong behavior works exactly as implemented.

The failure is not that AI cannot write tests. The failure is treating correlated output as independent evidence.

The Test Passed Because It Copied the Assumption

Imagine a billing requirement:

Apply a 20% discount to the order subtotal, then add tax to the discounted amount.

The intended calculation is:

subtotal = 100.00
discount = 20.00
taxable amount = 80.00
tax = 8.00
final total = 88.00

An agent misreads the requirement and applies the discount after tax:

export function calculateTotal(subtotal, taxRate, discountRate) {
  const tax = subtotal * taxRate;
  const discount = subtotal * discountRate;

  return subtotal + tax - discount;
}

For the simple values above, both formulas happen to return 88.00. A generated test passes:

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { calculateTotal } from "./billing.js";

describe("calculateTotal", () => {
  it("applies a discount and tax", () => {
    expect(calculateTotal(100, 0.1, 0.2)).toBe(88);
  });
});

The test looks reasonable. It even uses a concrete expected value.

But it does not distinguish the intended formula from the incorrect one.

Now introduce a fixed discount, tax exemptions, jurisdiction-specific rounding, or items with different tax classes. The shared assumption becomes a production billing bug.

Coverage Is Not an Oracle

Code coverage answers questions such as:

  • Was this line executed?
  • Was this branch visited?
  • Was this function called?

It does not answer:

  • Was the expected value correct?
  • Did the test encode the product requirement?
  • Would the test fail for a plausible wrong implementation?
  • Did the system preserve a business invariant?

A generated test suite can reach 100% line coverage while asserting the implementation's current behavior back at itself.

This pattern is especially weak:

const result = calculateTotal(order);

expect(result.subtotal).toBe(order.subtotal);
expect(result.tax).toBe(result.taxableAmount * order.taxRate);
expect(result.total).toBe(
  result.subtotal + result.tax - result.discount
);

The test reconstructs the same formula used by the implementation. If the formula is wrong, both sides remain wrong together.

A test needs an oracle: an independent reason to believe the expected result is correct.

Shared Context Creates Correlated Failures

When one agent writes the code and tests in the same session, both artifacts may inherit:

  • the same ambiguous requirement
  • the same incomplete repository context
  • the same mistaken domain assumption
  • the same missing edge case
  • the same naming-driven interpretation
  • the same outdated example

Regenerating the test in the same conversation may not add meaningful independence. The model still sees its earlier reasoning and implementation.

Even using a second model is not automatically enough. If both models receive the same ambiguous prompt and derive expectations from the same implementation, they can converge on the same attractive mistake.

The goal is not merely a different generator. The goal is a different source of truth.

The Dangerous Test Patterns

1. Asserting the implementation against itself 

expect(formatPrice(input)).toBe(formatPrice(input));

This extreme example is obvious, but indirect versions are common. A test may call the same helper, parser, mapper, or formula as the production path.

2. Snapshotting unknown behavior 

expect(calculateInvoice(order)).toMatchSnapshot();

The first snapshot records whatever the implementation produced. Approving it proves that someone accepted the output, not that the output matches the requirement.

Snapshots are useful for detecting change. They are weak at establishing initial correctness when nobody verifies their meaning.

3. Mirroring private implementation details 

expect(cache.internalEntries.size).toBe(1);

The test confirms structure rather than observable behavior. It may pass while users receive stale data, and fail during a safe refactor.

4. Testing only the example from the prompt

If an issue contains one example, an agent will often reproduce it as one happy-path test. That example may not distinguish competing interpretations.

5. Mocking away the failure 

paymentGateway.charge = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: "paid" });

The test proves behavior for a dependency that always succeeds instantly. It says nothing about timeouts, duplicated responses, uncertain outcomes, or retries after the remote side processed the charge.

A quick review question For every generated assertion, ask: > Where did this expected value come from? If the answer is "from the implementation," "from the agent's earlier output," or "from a snapshot we did not inspect," the test is not independent enough for a critical behavior.

Start With Invariants, Not Examples

Examples verify selected points. Invariants describe properties that must hold across many inputs.

For a discount calculation, useful invariants might include:

  • a discount cannot increase the pre-tax amount
  • a 0% discount changes nothing
  • a 100% discount produces no taxable amount
  • the total cannot be negative
  • changing item order cannot change the total
  • rounding happens at the boundary defined by the business rules

Property-based tests can exercise these rules across generated inputs:

import fc from "fast-check";
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { calculateTotal } from "./billing.js";

it("never increases the total when the discount increases", () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 100_000, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 0.3, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
      (subtotal, taxRate, firstDiscount, secondDiscount) => {
        const lower = Math.min(firstDiscount, secondDiscount);
        const higher = Math.max(firstDiscount, secondDiscount);

        const totalWithLowerDiscount = calculateTotal(
          subtotal,
          taxRate,
          lower
        );

        const totalWithHigherDiscount = calculateTotal(
          subtotal,
          taxRate,
          higher
        );

        expect(totalWithHigherDiscount).toBeLessThanOrEqual(
          totalWithLowerDiscount
        );
      }
    )
  );
});

This still does not prove every domain rule. It does make it harder for one convenient example to hide a broken relationship.

Derive Acceptance Tests From a Separate Source

The strongest acceptance tests should come from artifacts that existed independently of the implementation:

  • product acceptance criteria
  • API contracts
  • regulatory rules
  • protocol specifications
  • previously verified behavior
  • production examples approved by domain experts
  • compatibility fixtures from another implementation

For the billing example, create a decision table before asking an agent to implement it:

Case: percentage discount before tax
Subtotal: 125.00
Discount: 20%
Tax rate: 8%
Expected discount: 25.00
Expected taxable amount: 100.00
Expected tax: 8.00
Expected total: 108.00

Then convert that independently reviewed fixture into a test:

it("taxes the amount after the percentage discount", () => {
  expect(calculateTotal(125, 0.08, 0.2)).toBe(108);
});

The unusual values are deliberate. They distinguish formulas that coincidentally agree for simpler inputs.

Make the Test Fight the Implementation

Mutation testing changes the code in small ways and checks whether the tests fail.

For example, a mutation tool might replace:

const taxableAmount = subtotal - discount;

with:

const taxableAmount = subtotal + discount;

or change:

if (total >= freeShippingThreshold)

into:

if (total > freeShippingThreshold)

If the test suite stays green, it did not protect that behavior.

A mutation score is not a perfect quality metric. Equivalent mutations and costly test runs are real constraints. But targeted mutation testing is valuable for authorization, billing, retries, idempotency, limits, and other logic where a plausible one-character error matters.

Meta reported a related change-aware approach in its 2026 work on Just-in-Time catching tests. Instead of only generating tests that pass on the proposed code, catching tests are designed to surface regressions before a change lands. In an evaluation of 22,126 generated tests, change-aware methods improved candidate catch generation, and the reported process found confirmed serious failures. The important idea is practical: generated tests should actively try to falsify the change, not merely document it.

Use Differential Testing When You Have Two Implementations

Differential testing runs the same inputs through two independent implementations and compares the outputs.

This is useful during rewrites, migrations, and optimizations:

for (const order of generatedOrders) {
  const legacyResult = legacyCalculator(order);
  const newResult = newCalculator(order);

  expect(newResult).toEqual(legacyResult);
}

The reference implementation does not need to be fast or elegant. It needs to be trusted for the behavior under comparison.

Be careful: if the legacy behavior contains known bugs, encode those exceptions explicitly. Otherwise, differential testing can preserve defects just as snapshots do.

Separate the Roles in the Workflow

A safer AI-assisted workflow creates friction between implementation and validation.

Step 1: Extract the contract

Before generating code, write down:

  • inputs and outputs
  • invariants
  • boundary conditions
  • error behavior
  • security constraints
  • examples that distinguish plausible interpretations

Step 2: Generate the implementation

Give the coding agent the contract, but do not let its implementation become the source of expected values.

Step 3: Generate adversarial tests in a fresh context

Provide another agent or session with:

  • the contract
  • the code diff
  • public interfaces
  • known failure classes

Ask it to find counterexamples, not to improve coverage.

A useful prompt is:

Act as an adversarial test engineer.

Given the requirement and code diff:
1. List plausible incorrect interpretations.
2. Create inputs that distinguish them.
3. Identify boundary conditions and invariants.
4. Write tests that would fail for each plausible wrong implementation.
5. Do not derive expected values from the implementation under test.

Step 4: Run targeted mutation testing

Focus on critical decisions rather than mutating the entire repository on every commit.

Step 5: Review the oracle

Reviewers should spend less time asking whether the test is readable and more time asking:

  • Why is this expected value correct?
  • Which wrong implementation would this test reject?
  • Is the test independent of production helpers?
  • What happens at the exact boundary?
  • Which requirement remains untested?

Step 6: Keep merge controls

A green agent-generated pull request still needs repository protections, required checks, and human review. GitHub explicitly requires human review before merging draft pull requests produced by its coding agent and layers security scanning and branch restrictions around generated changes.

That is not ceremony. It is recognition that generated code plus generated tests is evidence, not authority.

A Practical Review Example

Suppose an agent adds this rate limiter:

export function isAllowed(requestCount, limit) {
  return requestCount <= limit;
}

It also generates:

it("allows requests within the limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(3, 5)).toBe(true);
});

it("blocks requests above the limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(6, 5)).toBe(false);
});

Both tests pass. Coverage may be complete.

But the critical question is whether the fifth request is allowed or whether limit represents the number of requests already consumed. The tests avoid the exact boundary where the interpretation matters.

Add the distinguishing case:

it("defines behavior at the exact limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(5, 5)).toBe(false);
});

Whether false is correct depends on the contract. The key is that a human or independent specification must decide it. The implementation cannot decide its own requirement.

Actionable Checklist

Before trusting AI-generated tests, verify that:

  • [ ] Expected values come from a specification, fixture, reference implementation, or reviewed calculation.
  • [ ] Tests do not call production helpers to calculate their own expectations.
  • [ ] Boundary values are tested explicitly.
  • [ ] At least one case distinguishes plausible interpretations of the requirement.
  • [ ] Important behavior is expressed as an invariant where possible.
  • [ ] Snapshots were inspected for meaning before approval.
  • [ ] Mocks include failures, delays, retries, and uncertain outcomes.
  • [ ] Generated tests attempt to falsify the change, not only confirm it.
  • [ ] Critical logic receives targeted mutation testing.
  • [ ] Rewrites are compared against a trusted implementation where appropriate.
  • [ ] A reviewer examines the test oracle, not only coverage.
  • [ ] Agent-created pull requests remain subject to required checks and human review.

CTA: Pick one AI-generated test from your current project and trace every expected value back to its source. If the trail ends at the implementation itself, replace that assertion with an independent fixture, invariant, or boundary case.

The Takeaway

AI-generated tests are useful. They can produce scaffolding, cover routine branches, explore edge cases, and shorten feedback loops.

But tests generated from the same context as the implementation are not automatically independent validation.

They may encode the same misunderstanding twice:

incorrect requirement interpretation
              ↓
      incorrect implementation
              ↓
     matching incorrect tests
              ↓
          green build

Do not measure confidence only by the number of generated tests or the coverage percentage.

Increase independence instead:

  • derive expectations from reviewed contracts
  • test invariants and exact boundaries
  • use fresh adversarial context
  • apply mutation and differential testing
  • review where each oracle came from
  • keep humans responsible for the merge decision

A test suite is valuable when it can disagree with the implementation.

What is the most convincing green test suite you have seen that still allowed a production bug through?

Sources

  • The Death of Traditional Testing: Agentic Development Broke a 50-Year-Old Field, JiTTesting Can Revive It
  • Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta
  • Risks and mitigations for GitHub Copilot cloud agent
