articles.body_html:
My smart light bulb tried to mine crypto last Tuesday.

Not a joke. Not a metaphor.

I have a cheap Tuya bulb I bought from for $12.99 in 2023. "Smart Life" app, WiFi enabled, 16 million colors, works with Alexa. I put it in my closet so I could say "closet on" and feel like I'm in .

At 3:17 AM, my network monitor woke me up. Not an alarm — just a little red dot on my Grafana dashboard. My closet bulb had uploaded 400MB of data to an IP address in Shenzhen and was now holding a persistent outbound connection on port 3333. Port 3333 is not for turning on lights. Port 3333 is for Monero mining pools.

I unplugged it. I took it apart. Inside was an ESP8266 clone, 2MB of flash, firmware from 2019 with a hardcoded Telnet password: admin:admin. And a little bonus binary called xmr_mini hidden in a partition that shouldn't exist.

That bulb was $13. It had no business having enough brains to betray me, but it did. And it's not alone. Your house is full of them.

Welcome to the Internet of Shit.

The Lie We All Bought

The IoT pitch was beautiful: everything connected, everything smart, everything effortless.

The reality is this: a $400 billion industry built on the cheapest possible chips, running the oldest possible Linux kernels, written by the lowest bidder, shipped with default credentials that haven't changed since 2008.

Here's the math that kills you:

A company wants to sell a smart plug for $9.99.

  • The ESP8266 chip costs $0.89
  • The relay costs $0.40
  • The plastic costs $0.30
  • The profit margin needs to be $4

Where do you think they cut costs? Security audits? Code review? A firmware update server?

No. They cut everything.

They take the SDK example code from Espressif that says // TODO: CHANGE DEFAULT PASSWORD, they don't change the default password, they compile it, and they ship 500,000 units.

I've dumped firmware from 23 different IoT devices in the last year. Light bulbs, cameras, doorbells, pet feeders, a smart toaster — yes, a toaster that can run Doom and also get botnetted.

Here is what I find, every single time:

1. Telnet or SSH open with root:root or admin:admin
In 2026. After Mirai. After 8 years of us screaming about Mirai.

2. A web server running as root from 2016
With a CVE list longer than my grocery list. No update mechanism. Ever.

3. Hardcoded MQTT credentials
One username and password for every device they ever sold. mqtt_user: TuyaSmart123! — I found that in 4 different brands.

4. Cloud buckets with no auth
Your camera footage, your voice clips, your WiFi password — sitting in an open S3 bucket because the intern left public: true in the config.

This isn't a bug. This is the business model.

My Living Room Botnet Census

I got angry after the light bulb thing, so I did what any normal person does: I turned my apartment into a surveillance state for my own devices.

I took that $26 GL.iNet Mango router — the little yellow travel router everyone buys for hotel WiFi — and I made it my border guard.

I flashed it with OpenWrt. Put it between my modem and my real router. Installed:

  • Pi-hole to DNS-blackhole every ad, tracker, and telemetry domain
  • AdGuard Home as backup
  • Suricata in IDS mode to watch what my devices actually say

Then I let it run for 7 days. I didn't block anything. I just watched.

Here is what my "smart" home does when I'm not looking:

My $35 Wyze camera: Pings wyze-log.s3.amazonaws.com every 30 seconds, even when I have "record only on motion" turned off. Uploaded 2.1GB in a week. Of what? I'm not recording 2.1GB of my living room wall.

My smart TV (TCL ): At 2am every night, it resolves 47 different ad domains. It tried to reach doubleclick.net 14,000 times in 7 days. Fourteen thousand. It also sends my WiFi SSID and a list of nearby SSIDs to Roku every 6 hours. Why does Roku need to know my neighbor's WiFi name?

My robot vacuum: Sent a compressed map of my apartment — literally a floorplan of where my bed is — to a server in Singapore. The privacy policy says "to improve cleaning." My bed doesn't need to be in Singapore.

My wife's smart toothbrush: Yes, this exists. It sends brush time, pressure, and location to . 19 times a day.

The worst offender? A $19 smart plug from a brand that doesn't exist anymore. It tried to SSH into my NAS. My own plug tried to brute force my own NAS on my local network. Because its firmware had Mirai's old dictionary baked in and it scans /24s automatically.

We put computers that actively attack other computers inside our houses and then act surprised when they do.

Why Your Router is Lying to You

Your ISP router is not a router. It's a plastic box designed to blink green so you stop calling tech support.

It does NAT. It does WiFi badly. It does not inspect traffic. It does not tell you that your light bulb is mining Monero. It will never tell you.

You need a watchtower.

This is why I tell everyone to build a $20 SOC — Security Operations Center. It sounds insane. SOCs are for enterprises with 6 monitors and cold brew on tap. But a $20 SOC is just a tiny Linux box that sits and judges all your other boxes.

The Mango costs $20-26 on Amazon. Total build with a USB stick for logs is under $30. It draws 2 watts. It has no subscription. It will outlive your smart fridge.

What it gives you:

  • Visibility. For the first time, you see that your bulb is talking to 45.76.123.89 at 3am. That alone is worth it.
  • Blocking at the root. Pi-hole kills ads, trackers, and 80% of malware C2 domains before they even leave your house. Your TV gets dumber — which is good. Dumb TVs can't snitch.
  • Receipts. When that bulb gets popped, you have logs. When you call the manufacturer and they say "impossible," you send them a pcap. They shut up very fast.

The second part of my setup is even more paranoid: an offline box.

I have a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W — $35 if you're lucky — running a local LLM completely offline. No WiFi, no cloud. I call it the Blackbox. I feed it suspicious firmware dumps, weird log lines, long ToS documents I don't want to upload to ChatGPT. It summarizes, it finds hardcoded creds, it writes abuse emails. Nothing ever leaves my apartment.

When you're dissecting a light bulb that tried to rob you, you don't want to paste its private key into someone else's cloud.

The Fix Isn't What You Think

People want me to say "don't buy smart devices." That's not realistic. I'm not going to hand-wash dishes because my dishwasher has WiFi.

The fix is hostile architecture. Treat every IoT device like it's already compromised, because statistically, it is.

My rules now:

1. VLAN or it didn't happen. All IoT shit goes on its own WiFi network that can't talk to my laptops, NAS, or phones. The Mango makes this 3 clicks. Your main router probably doesn't. That's why you need the Mango.

2. No internet unless it proves it needs it. My light bulbs don't need internet to turn on. I block their internet at DNS level. If they stop working, good — I return them and buy ones that work locally with Home Assistant or ESPHome. If a light bulb requires the cloud to turn on, it's not a light bulb, it's a subscription to light.

3. Flash or trash. If a device runs ESP8266/ESP32, I flash it with Tasmota or ESPHome immediately. Open firmware, local control, no cloud, no mystery binaries. It takes 10 minutes and it turns a spy into a tool. If I can't flash it, I don't buy it.

4. Assume default passwords. First thing I do with any new device: nmap it. nmap -p 23,22,80,8080 <its IP>. If Telnet is open, I try admin/admin, root/root, admin/password. It works 60% of the time. I then change it or brick it.

5. Log everything for 7 days. When you get a new device, put it in the watchtower and just watch. If it phones home 14,000 times, you know.

The IoT industry will not fix itself. There is no incentive. A $13 bulb that is secure costs $15. And $15 loses to $13 on Amazon every time. Security is invisible until it fails, and failure is externalized onto you.

The only person who can secure your house is you. And it doesn't take a $10,000 rack. It takes $26, a USB stick, and the willingness to accept that your smart home is actually a very dumb botnet that you happen to live in.

My closet light is now running ESPHome. It turns on. It turns off. It doesn't mine crypto. It doesn't talk to Shenzhen. It took me 20 minutes to flash.

It is the only smart device in my house I trust.

The rest are in jail.

Want to build the same jail I use?

This is the exact defensive stack from this story — the parts lists, flash commands, Pi-hole blocklists, and Suricata rules I use so my own light bulbs can't betray me:

The $20 SOC: Build a Tiny Defensive Network Monitor — The Mango build, step-by-step. How to put a Pi-hole + IDS between your modem and your whole house, VLAN your IoT, and finally see what your TV does at 2am. My live configs and power measurements inside: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/20dollarsoxc

BUILD THE BLACKBOX: An Offline AI Field Terminal That Works When Nothing Else Does — The Pi Zero that runs Phi-3/Gemma locally with no cloud. I use it to dissect firmware, parse logs, and draft abuse reports without ever sending your home data to OpenAI: numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/blackbox-offline-ai

articles.title: The Bug Lives at the Seam, Not in the Logic
articles.description: The encrypted secret was bytes. It round-tripped perfectly in the in-memory store. The unit tests...
articles.body_html:
The encrypted secret was bytes. It round-tripped perfectly in the in-memory store. The unit tests passed. In Postgres, the column was JSON, and bytes is not JSON-serializable. The secret store blew up at the one boundary the in-memory test never crossed.

That was the pattern of the entire v0.2.0 field test on HivePlane. The hard part wasn't the logic — it was the data model and the boundaries. Every defect was a value that was fine in Python and broke one step later, at a persistence seam.

This is the article about tracing each value across every persistence boundary — because the bug lives one boundary further than your unit test.

One defect per seam-type

Defect The value that crossed the seam Where it broke
D-5 Secret ciphertext as bytes Postgres JSON persistence rejected binary
D-7 A desired_specs row keyed by id Second source hit a PK collision — id vs uniqueness
D-8 The kill-switch record existed GET /tools/disabled listed enabled tools — state vs record
D-9 A workload with runs, deleted Raw FK violation 500 instead of a 409 with a reason
#573 A backup manifest pinning alembic_head=0034 Schema head was 0035 — restore against the wrong schema

Read that table as the taxonomy. The seam, not the logic, is where each one failed.

The bytes that broke JSON

D-5 was the cleanest example. The encrypted secret vault stored ciphertext as bytes. In the in-memory store, it round-tripped perfectly. The unit tests passed. In Postgres, the column was JSON, and bytes is not JSON-serializable. The secret store blew up at the persistence boundary — the one place the in-memory test never exercised.

The fix wasn't in the model; it was at the boundary: base64-encode the ciphertext on the way to Postgres, decode on the way back. The model stays bytes. The seam learns to translate. The unit test that uses the in-memory store still passes — and still proves nothing about the seam.

tip: Your in-memory store and your Postgres store share an interface, not a serialization. A value that round-trips in memory can fail at the JSON column. Trace the value across the boundary the in-memory test never crosses.

The second source that broke the first

D-7 was an id-versus-uniqueness confusion. The reconcile loader keyed desired_specs by id. One source worked. A second source, applying the same desired state, hit a primary-key violation — because the row already existed, and the key assumed one source. The uniqueness constraint and the id were the same field, and they meant different things.

The fix is composite keys and idempotent upserts: (source_id, workload_id). A second source is a second row, not a collision. The bug only appears when you have two sources, which is why the single-source field test never caught it.

The enabled tool that was "disabled"

D-8 was a state-versus-record confusion that I still find funny. GET /tools/disabled returned a list that included enabled tools. The kill-switch record existed in the table; the tool was not actually disabled. The endpoint reported the record, not the state. A "disabled tools" list that includes enabled tools is worse than no list — it trains the operator to ignore it.

The fix: the endpoint reports the state, derived from the record and the current tool status, not the record alone. A record of a disable that was later reversed is history, not a current fact.

The FK that returned 500

D-9 was the database teaching me API design. Deleting a workload that had runs returned a 500 — a raw foreign-key violation surfacing as an internal error. The caller got a server error; the operator got no reason. The fix is a 409 with "workload has N runs; delete the runs first or cascade." A constraint violation is a user-facing condition, not a server fault. The seam between the database and the API is where a 500 becomes a 409.

The schema head the manifest lied about

573 was the one that could have been catastrophic. A backup manifest pinned alembic_head to 0034. The live schema head was 0035. A restore would have succeeded — the manifest said the schemas matched — against a database that was one migration ahead. The restore verified the manifest's claim, not the world's truth.

The fix: the restore verifies the actual schema head against the manifest, and refuses a mismatch. A manifest that lies about its own head is a backup that restores you to the wrong version of your own system.

What I learned

Trace each value across every persistence boundary: binary-vs-JSON, global-key-vs-tenant-scope, id-vs-uniqueness, state-vs-record, FK-vs-409, manifest-head-vs-schema-head. A unit test that stops at the seam passes; the bug lives one boundary further. The Postgres-gated tests — the ones CI runs with a database — are the ones that catch it. And a constraint violation is a user condition, not a server fault: the seam between the database and the API is where 500 becomes 409 with a reason.

The v0.2.0 field test runs zero-skip against the real stack with real PostgreSQL — 36/36 scenarios, 67/67 container tests — and the defect ledger (D-1…D-11) is the evidence that the seams, not the logic, were the work. Full receipts in the field-test report and the Docker test report.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36) · Docker report (67/67)
  • Migration guide (v0.1.0 → v0.2.0)
  • State store design

Pick one value in your system and trace it from the model to the Postgres column to the API response. Where does it change shape? That's where your next bug is — and where your unit test stops.

articles.title: Add a Link Preview Smoke Test to Your Deploy Pipeline (Node Script + GitHub Actions)
articles.description: We test our APIs, our components, and sometimes our CSS. Then a release goes out, marketing drops the...
articles.body_html:
We test our APIs, our components, and sometimes our CSS. Then a release goes out, marketing drops the new page into a Slack channel and a LinkedIn post, and the card shows last month's image with a title that ends in "| Home".

Link previews break silently. No error page, no failed request in your logs, nothing in Sentry. The first signal is usually a screenshot from someone outside the team. So I started treating the share card like any other contract and testing it after deploy.

This post walks through a small, dependency-free Node script that checks the Open Graph and Twitter Card tags on a list of production URLs, plus a GitHub Actions job that runs it after each deploy.

What's worth asserting

You don't need to test everything in the <head>. The failures I see most often are:

  1. og:title, og:description, or og:image missing from the first HTML response (often because they're set client-side).
  2. og:image is relative, points at localhost or a staging host, or doesn't return an image.
  3. Duplicate og:title / og:image tags from two plugins or two layout levels.
  4. og:url pointing at the wrong environment.
  5. twitter:card missing when you actually want the large image layout on X.

All of those are visible in raw HTML, which is exactly what crawlers read. Most social crawlers don't execute JavaScript, so the test shouldn't either. A plain fetch is closer to reality than a headless browser.

The script

Save this as scripts/check-previews.mjs. It uses Node 18+'s built-in fetch, so there's nothing to install.

// scripts/check-previews.mjs
const BASE = process.env.SITE_URL ?? "https://example.com";
const PATHS = ["/", "/pricing", "/blog/latest-post"];
const UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; PreviewSmokeTest/1.0)";

function metaAll(html, key) {
  // Matches property="og:x" or name="twitter:x", either attribute order
  const re = new RegExp(
    `<meta[^>]+(?:property|name)=["']${key}["'][^>]*>`, "gi");
  return [...html.matchAll(re)].map((m) => {
    const c = m[0].match(/content=["']([^"']*)["']/i);
    return c ? c[1] : "";
  });
}

async function checkImage(url) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { "User-Agent": UA }, redirect: "follow" });
  const type = res.headers.get("content-type") ?? "";
  const size = Number(res.headers.get("content-length") ?? 0);
  return { ok: res.ok && type.startsWith("image/"), status: res.status, type, size };
}

async function checkPage(path) {
  const url = new URL(path, BASE).toString();
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { "User-Agent": UA } });
  const html = await res.text();
  const errors = [];

  for (const key of ["og:title", "og:description", "og:image", "og:url"]) {
    const values = metaAll(html, key);
    if (values.length === 0) errors.push(`${key} missing`);
    if (values.length > 1) errors.push(`${key} appears ${values.length} times`);
  }

  const [image] = metaAll(html, "og:image");
  if (image) {
    if (!image.startsWith("https://")) errors.push(`og:image not absolute https: ${image}`);
    if (/localhost|staging|vercel\.app/.test(image)) errors.push(`og:image points at non-prod host: ${image}`);
    else {
      const img = await checkImage(new URL(image, url).toString());
      if (!img.ok) errors.push(`og:image fetch failed (${img.status}, ${img.type})`);
      if (img.size > 1_000_000) errors.push(`og:image is ${Math.round(img.size / 1024)} KB`);
    }
  }

  const [ogUrl] = metaAll(html, "og:url");
  if (ogUrl && !ogUrl.startsWith(BASE)) errors.push(`og:url is ${ogUrl}`);

  if (metaAll(html, "twitter:card").length === 0) errors.push("twitter:card missing");

  return { url, status: res.status, errors };
}

const results = await Promise.all(PATHS.map(checkPage));
let failed = 0;
for (const r of results) {
  if (r.status !== 200 || r.errors.length) {
    failed++;
    console.error(`âœ— ${r.url} (HTTP ${r.status})`);
    r.errors.forEach((e) => console.error(`   - ${e}`));
  } else {
    console.log(`âœ“ ${r.url}`);
  }
}
process.exit(failed ? 1 : 0);

Run it locally against production:

SITE_URL=https://yoursite.com node scripts/check-previews.mjs

A few design choices worth calling out:

  • Regex instead of a DOM parser. For <meta> tags in a server-rendered head this is good enough and keeps the script dependency-free. If your HTML is unusual (unquoted attributes, tags split across lines with odd spacing), swap in node-html-parser or cheerio.
  • Duplicate detection. Two og:image tags is one of the most common real-world bugs, especially with CMS plugins or nested layouts. Crawlers pick one, and it's often not the one you want.
  • The size check uses content-length. Some servers don't send it for images; that's fine, the check just passes. Tighten it if you care.
  • twitter:card is enforced. X can fall back to Open Graph for title, description and image, but the card layout itself comes from twitter:card. If you want summary_large_image, say so. Delete that line if you don't post to X.

Running it after every deploy

The test has to hit the deployed site, so it belongs after your deploy step, not in the unit test job. Here's a minimal GitHub Actions workflow triggered after a successful deployment:

# .github/workflows/preview-smoke.yml
name: Link preview smoke test
on:
  deployment_status:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  previews:
    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: node scripts/check-previews.mjs
        env:
          SITE_URL: ${{ github.event.deployment_status.environment_url || 'https://yoursite.com' }}

Hosts like Vercel and Netlify emit deployment_status events, so this runs automatically for previews and production. For preview deployments, you may want to relax the "non-prod host" rule, since the image URL will legitimately point at the preview domain.

What the script won't tell you

An automated check proves the tags exist and the image loads. It doesn't tell you whether the card looks right: whether the headline gets cut off mid-word, whether the important part of the image survives a wide crop, whether the description reads like a sentence or a keyword list.

For that, I still eyeball the card before any launch that matters. I use OG Scope, a free checker I built for this. Paste the public URL and it fetches the HTML server-side (no JavaScript, same as the crawlers), then shows estimated cards for LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Facebook, X, Slack, Discord and Telegram, a metadata table, an image check, and a short checklist. No account needed. The cards are estimates, not the platforms' own renders, so for a stale cache you still go to Facebook's Sharing Debugger or LinkedIn's Post Inspector.

The split works well in practice: the script guards against regressions on every deploy, and a human looks at the card when the stakes are high.

Extending it

Ideas once the basic version is running:

  • Read PATHS from your sitemap so new pages get covered automatically.
  • Assert og:title length (around 60 characters is a reasonable ceiling before truncation).
  • Check that og:image changed when your hero image changed, to catch stale cached URLs.
  • Post failures to a Slack channel instead of only failing the job.

It's a tiny amount of code for a bug class that otherwise only gets reported by your users. Worth an afternoon.

Abid Ali is a web developer in Pakistan who builds small developer tools. He made OG Scope to check link previews before they go out.

articles.title: Copy a remote video into R2 from a Cloudflare Worker without buffering it
articles.description: If your Worker copies files it didn't create (AI generation results, imports from a URL, exports from...
articles.body_html:
If your Worker copies files it didn't create (AI generation results, imports from a URL, exports from another service), the obvious line, await res.arrayBuffer(), loads the whole file into an isolate whose 128 MB is shared by every request it is serving. For video that's the wrong default. You can stream the file straight from the source into R2 instead, and it takes three pieces: FixedLengthStream, pipeTo, and an S3 PUT signed as UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD.

The code below is trimmed from the copy step at Movoa, which moves each finished video from a provider's temporary URL into our own bucket.

TL;DR

  • Workers memory is 128 MB per isolate, not per request, so buffered copies add up across concurrent requests.
  • Stream when the source sends Content-Length: response.body.pipeTo(new FixedLengthStream(length).writable) and PUT the readable side.
  • Sign the stream with aws4fetch; it uses UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, which R2's S3 API accepts over HTTPS.
  • Reject tiny bodies before writing, and fall back to buffering only when there's no length (or you're in Node).

Why buffering is the trap

The tempting version is three lines:

const res = await fetch(resultUrl);
const body = new Uint8Array(await res.arrayBuffer());
await bucket.put(key, body);

Cloudflare's limits page (read 2026-10-16) is specific about why this bites: each isolate "can consume up to 128 MB of memory", and "this limit is per-isolate, not per-invocation. A single isolate can handle many concurrent requests." When an isolate goes over, in-flight requests are allowed to finish and new requests go to a fresh isolate; under heavy load some incoming requests can be cancelled.

So the risk isn't one big file. It's two or three ordinary video files being copied by the same isolate at the same moment, each fully materialised in memory.

The PUT needs a length, so stream only when you have one

A single S3 PUT to R2 wants a Content-Length. A raw ReadableStream doesn't carry one, which is where FixedLengthStream comes in. It's a Workers runtime TransformStream that you construct with the expected byte count: it tells the runtime the body's length up front, and it errors if the bytes that flow through don't match. That second property is a truncation check: if the source sends fewer than length bytes, the stream errors and the upload fails instead of leaving half a file in your bucket.

Here is the streaming branch, lightly trimmed from our code:

const response = await fetch(url, {
  headers,                 // forward auth if the result URL needs it
  redirect: 'follow',
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
});
if (!response.ok || !response.body) return fail(`HTTP ${response.status}`);

const contentType = response.headers.get('content-type') || 'application/octet-stream';
const length = Number(response.headers.get('content-length') || NaN);

const FixedLength = (globalThis as any).FixedLengthStream; // only exists on workerd
if (FixedLength && Number.isFinite(length) && length > 0) {
  if (length < minBytes) {
    void response.body.cancel().catch(() => {});
    return fail(`too small (${length} bytes)`);
  }
  const { readable, writable } = new FixedLength(length);
  const piping = response.body.pipeTo(writable);   // source → FixedLengthStream
  const result = await putStream(env, { body: readable, length, key, contentType });
  await piping.catch(() => {});                    // surface nothing twice
  return result;
}

Two details matter. The pipeTo promise is started but not awaited before the PUT, because the PUT is what drains the readable side; awaiting the pipe first would deadlock. And the feature check on globalThis.FixedLengthStream keeps the same module working under Node in local dev, where that class doesn't exist (more on that below).

Signing a body you haven't read

R2 speaks the S3 API, so the PUT is a signed request. SigV4 normally includes a hash of the payload, which is impossible for bytes you haven't received yet. aws4fetch handles this by signing a stream body as UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and R2 accepts that over HTTPS:

import { AwsClient } from 'aws4fetch';

// env: R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID, R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (an R2 API token),
// R2_ENDPOINT = https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, R2_BUCKET
async function putStream(env, { body, length, key, contentType }) {
  const client = new AwsClient({
    accessKeyId: env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
    secretAccessKey: env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
    region: 'auto',
    service: 's3',
  });
  const res = await client.fetch(`${env.R2_ENDPOINT}/${env.R2_BUCKET}/${key}`, {
    method: 'PUT',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': contentType,
      'Content-Length': String(length),
    },
    body,                              // the FixedLengthStream readable
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const detail = (await res.text().catch(() => '')).slice(0, 200);
    return fail(`Upload failed: ${res.status} ${detail}`);
  }
  return { success: true, key, url: publicUrlFor(key) };
}

Checks before you write anything

  • A 200 that is really an error. Some providers answer the result URL with a short JSON error and a 200 status when a file isn't ready or has expired. A minBytes threshold checked against Content-Length catches that before anything is written; cancel the body so the connection is released.
  • Redirects and auth. Signed result URLs often redirect to object storage. Set redirect: 'follow' and pass through whatever headers the provider requires.
  • Timeouts. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) on the fetch keeps a stalled source from holding the request open indefinitely. We give the whole download-and-upload 100 seconds.

What about the R2 binding?

If your Worker has the bucket bound (env.BUCKET), put() accepts a ReadableStream too. The catch is the same: the stream needs a known length, which a fetch() response body with a Content-Length has, and the readable side of a FixedLengthStream has. So await env.BUCKET.put(key, response.body) streams when the source sends a length; for anything else, wrap it in FixedLengthStream first.

We use the S3 API instead because the same storage module also runs under Node (local dev and scripts), where there is no binding, and one signed-request path serves both.

When you can't stream

Two cases still take the buffered path:

  1. The source sends no Content-Length (chunked transfer). Without a length there's nothing to give FixedLengthStream, and a single PUT can't be sent. Buffering is the simple answer; for large files, a multipart upload with fixed-size parts is the scalable one.
  2. Local development under Node (next dev, next start), where FixedLengthStream isn't defined. The feature check routes these to arrayBuffer(), which is fine on a laptop. 
// No length, or not on workerd: buffer, and know this is the memory path.
const body = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
if (body.length < minBytes) return fail(`too small (${body.length} bytes)`);
return uploadFile({ body, key, contentType });

Checklist

  • Check response.ok and Content-Length before touching storage.
  • On workerd with a known length: pipeTo into new FixedLengthStream(length), PUT the readable side, then settle the pipe promise.
  • Sign with aws4fetch (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD); send Content-Length explicitly.
  • Reject bodies under a sane minimum; follow redirects; set a timeout.
  • Buffer only as the fallback, and treat it as the path that costs memory.

On the streaming branch the file never sits in your isolate's memory, and a short read fails loudly instead of saving half a video. The buffered branch is the exception you keep for chunked sources and local dev.

The videos this copies come from the Movoa video generator, which turns one sentence or a photo into a clip with sound; the first one is free and needs no account.

articles.title: An incident report nobody could open, an extension that wanted my token, and 80 lines instead
articles.description: The report nobody could open   We write incident reports as single HTML files: inline CSS,...
articles.body_html:
The report nobody could open

We write incident reports as single HTML files: inline CSS, an inline SVG timeline, no build step, one file you can read in ten years. They live in a private GitHub repository next to the code they are about.

Nobody could open them. GitHub shows an .html file as source, and the "download it, then double-click it" workflow is where reading stops for most people. GitHub Pages would render them, but Pages on a private repository is an Enterprise feature. GitHub's PDF viewer exists, but these are not PDFs.

The extension that wanted my token

There is a Chrome extension for exactly this problem. I read its code before installing it. It asks for a GitHub token (a personal access token, or an OAuth grant with full repo scope), sends that token to the author's server, and the server fetches your file and renders it on the author's domain.

That is a lot of trust for a preview button. An incident report is the most sensitive document a team writes, and the fix was to hand the key to the whole repository to a stranger's Lambda.

The other option, a userscript, keeps the token in the browser but resolves the short-lived tokenised link GitHub issues for a private file and passes it, as a URL parameter, to the author's website, which loads the file from there. The link to your private file lands in that site's address bar, history and hosting logs.

Both are honest projects, and the idea of a button beside Raw is theirs. I just did not want the file to leave the browser.

The Raw button already does the hard part

Click Raw on a private file and watch the network tab. GitHub answers github.com/<owner>/<repo>/raw/<ref>/<path> with your own session, then redirects to raw.githubusercontent.com with a token that expires in minutes. That host serves the file as text/plain, which is why it is never rendered, and sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. And github.com's Content Security Policy allows connections to it.

So a script running on the file page can do what Raw does, and then fix the only thing that was wrong, the content type:

const tab = window.open('', '_blank');                    // open inside the click, so popup blockers allow it
const response = await fetch(location.pathname.replace('/blob/', '/raw/'), { credentials: 'same-origin' });
const html = await response.text();
tab.location.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([html], { type: 'text/html' }));

That is the whole mechanism. The only network request is the one GitHub itself makes for Raw. No server, no token, no account, no site other than github.com in the path. The rendered page lives at a blob: URL in your browser, with no cookies and no access to GitHub.

80 lines instead

The result is unraw: a userscript that adds an unraw button next to Raw on every .html file page, and a bookmarklet for people who do not want to install anything. The button copies Raw's classes and data-* attributes so it matches GitHub's current styling, and a MutationObserver puts it back after GitHub's client-side navigation. The rest is the snippet above with error handling. Your userscript manager shows you all of it before installing; it is about 80 lines.

Two limits, both inherent to the approach. Pages that reference relative files (./style.css, img/x.png) render without them, because those paths do not exist at a blob: URL; self-contained pages render completely, and inlining is the right habit for documents you want to read from GitHub anyway. Inline scripts run inside the blob: page, isolated from GitHub, so treat a preview the way you would treat opening a downloaded copy.

The rule that produced the tool is the rule that keeps it small: the file may not leave your browser. Anything that would need a server or a token will not be added.

  • Install page, with the bookmarklet: https://thangaram611.github.io/unraw/
  • Userscript on Greasy Fork: https://greasyfork.org/scripts/600316-unraw
  • Source, MIT, with a comparison table drawn from each tool's code: https://github.com/thangaram611/unraw

articles.title: How to check your own IBKR statement for revenge trades
articles.description: Your broker shows a monthly total. It does not show which habit produced it.  I don't have a public...
articles.body_html:
Your broker shows a monthly total. It does not show which habit produced it.

I don't have a public track record to show, so the example below uses a made-up statement: 88 closing trades over four weeks, generated with random P&L and a deliberate penalty for trades right after a loss. Treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as real trading results.

On that file, 10 trades closed within 15 minutes of a loss. Together they lost $953, which is -$95 per trade. All 78 other trades averaged +$49 each. The month still ended at +$2,896, so the monthly total hid the pattern.

Here is the method, so you can run it on your own file.

1. Export the right file

In IBKR: Performance & Reports, Statements, Activity, run as CSV. The file has a Trades section. Each row with DataDiscriminator = Order is one fill. Rows with ClosedLot repeat the same fill at lot level, so skip them or you count twice.

2. Keep only closing trades

A closing trade has a non-zero Realized P/L. Opening trades show 0.

3. Flag the ones that follow a loss

Sort closing trades by time. Walk through them and remember the time of the last loss. Any closing trade within 15 minutes of that time goes in the "after a loss" group. Everything else is the baseline group.

let lastLoss = null, after = [], rest = [];
for (const t of closes) {
  if (lastLoss !== null && t.time - lastLoss <= 15 * 60000) after.push(t);
  else rest.push(t);
  if (t.pl < 0) lastLoss = t.time;
}

Note that a loss inside the window restarts the clock. A bad streak counts as one episode.

4. Compare averages, not totals

Total P&L after a loss depends on how many trades you took. Compare the average per trade in each group.

How to read the result

  • If the after-loss average is clearly worse than the baseline over 20 or more trades, the habit costs you money. Try a rule: after a loss, no new order for 15 minutes.
  • If the two averages are close, the habit is not your problem. Look at time of day or symbol next.
  • Under about 10 trades in the after-loss group, the number is noise. Do not change anything yet.

This does not tell you what to buy or sell. It describes what already happened.

Skip the code

I put the same checks in a page that runs in your browser. You drop in the CSV, the file stays on your computer, and there is no signup: https://ab-autopsy.agentbets.workers.dev/?utm_source=devto#try

It reports closed trades, net P&L, win rate, fees, the after-loss group, your worst hour and worst symbol. It only reads the Trades section of an IBKR Activity Statement CSV. I have only tested it on a made-up file like the one above; if it fails on yours, tell me in the comments which column looked different.

Who should skip it: if you trade under about 20 times a month, there is too little data for any of these splits.

articles.title: How to Pause Offscreen Animations Without Breaking the Experience
articles.description: Animation rarely breaks because pause() is difficult to call. It breaks because several different...
articles.body_html:
Animation rarely breaks because pause() is difficult to call. It breaks because several different things can cause motion to stop, and the implementation forgets why it stopped.

Imagine an animated hero that leaves the viewport. You pause it so a render loop is not running several screens below the fold. While it is offscreen, the user switches tabs, their reduced-motion preference is active, or they had already pressed a pause control. When the element returns, blindly calling play() can override one of those states.

A more reliable model is to treat viewport visibility as one input rather than the final decision. Collect the states that matter, derive one shouldAnimate value, and let the animation engine respond to that value.

const shouldAnimate =
  inViewport &&
  pageVisible &&
  motionAllowed &&
  !userPaused;

That small separation is what keeps an offscreen optimization from turning into a resume bug.

Pausing is easy. Resuming correctly is harder

A basic offscreen optimization often starts with IntersectionObserver:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
  if (entry.isIntersecting) {
    animation.play();
  } else {
    animation.pause();
  }
});

For a small decorative effect, this may be enough. It becomes fragile once the animation participates in more than one lifecycle.

Viewport visibility answers one question: is this element intersecting the viewport or another observer root? It does not tell you whether the browser tab is hidden, whether the user prefers reduced motion, whether a manual pause button is active, or whether another part of the application has suspended the effect.

isIntersecting is one input, not the final decision. The final decision should belong to your application state, while the animation engine only needs to know whether it should currently run.

Treat visibility as several independent signals

IntersectionObserver is a good starting point because the browser can report when an element enters or leaves the observer root. That makes it useful for sections that should stop doing animation work while they are away from the viewport.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
  ([entry]) => {
    setInViewport(entry.isIntersecting);
  },
  {
    threshold: 0,
  }
);

The observer only knows about the element's intersection geometry. If the user switches to another browser tab while the animated section remains inside the viewport, that is a separate document-level state.

The Page Visibility API gives you that signal:

function handleVisibilityChange() {
  setPageVisible(document.visibilityState === "visible");
}

document.addEventListener(
  "visibilitychange",
  handleVisibilityChange
);

Browsers already apply their own background-tab optimizations. MDN notes that requestAnimationFrame() callbacks are typically paused in background tabs in most browsers. That still does not solve element-level offscreen work while the document itself remains visible, which is why viewport and document visibility are useful as separate signals.

Reduced motion should also remain separate. prefers-reduced-motion represents a user preference around non-essential motion. It may incidentally reduce work, but performance is not the reason the preference exists.

const media = window.matchMedia(
  "(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)"
);

function handleMotionPreference() {
  setMotionAllowed(!media.matches);
}

media.addEventListener(
  "change",
  handleMotionPreference
);

User intent is the fourth state worth preserving. If somebody explicitly pauses an animation, scrolling it out of view and back again should not normally erase that choice.

With those states separated, the animation engine only has to answer one question: run or stop.

Build the run gate before the animation adapter

The easiest way to create state conflicts is to let every event handler control playback directly. The intersection callback pauses the effect, the visibility listener pauses it again, then one of them resumes it while another condition still says it should remain stopped.

A better architecture lets each event update only the state it owns. One derived value then becomes the source of truth. Here is a React hook for that layer:

"use client";

import {
  Dispatch,
  RefCallback,
  SetStateAction,
  useCallback,
  useEffect,
  useState,
} from "react";

type UseAnimationGateOptions = {
  rootMargin?: string;
  threshold?: number | number[];
};

type UseAnimationGateResult = {
  ref: RefCallback<Element>;
  shouldAnimate: boolean;
  inViewport: boolean;
  pageVisible: boolean;
  motionAllowed: boolean;
  userPaused: boolean;
  setUserPaused: Dispatch<SetStateAction<boolean>>;
};

export function useAnimationGate(
  options: UseAnimationGateOptions = {}
): UseAnimationGateResult {
  const {
    rootMargin = "0px",
    threshold = 0,
  } = options;

  const [element, setElement] = useState<Element | null>(null);
  const [inViewport, setInViewport] = useState(false);
  const [pageVisible, setPageVisible] = useState(true);
  const [motionAllowed, setMotionAllowed] = useState(true);
  const [userPaused, setUserPaused] = useState(false);

  const ref = useCallback<RefCallback<Element>>((node) => {
    setElement(node);
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!element) return;

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      ([entry]) => {
        setInViewport(entry.isIntersecting);
      },
      {
        rootMargin,
        threshold,
      }
    );

    observer.observe(element);

    return () => {
      observer.disconnect();
    };
  }, [element, rootMargin, threshold]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const updatePageVisibility = () => {
      setPageVisible(
        document.visibilityState === "visible"
      );
    };

    updatePageVisibility();

    document.addEventListener(
      "visibilitychange",
      updatePageVisibility
    );

    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener(
        "visibilitychange",
        updatePageVisibility
      );
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const media = window.matchMedia(
      "(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)"
    );

    const updateMotionPreference = () => {
      setMotionAllowed(!media.matches);
    };

    updateMotionPreference();

    media.addEventListener(
      "change",
      updateMotionPreference
    );

    return () => {
      media.removeEventListener(
        "change",
        updateMotionPreference
      );
    };
  }, []);

  const shouldAnimate =
    inViewport &&
    pageVisible &&
    motionAllowed &&
    !userPaused;

  return {
    ref,
    shouldAnimate,
    inViewport,
    pageVisible,
    motionAllowed,
    userPaused,
    setUserPaused,
  };
}

Using a callback ref here avoids assuming that the observed DOM node will never change. If React attaches the ref to a different node, the observer effect receives the new element and cleans up the old observer.

The hook still does not know whether the visual layer uses CSS, requestAnimationFrame, Web Animations, GSAP, or WebGL. That separation is deliberate. Visibility policy belongs above the rendering implementation.

Use IntersectionObserver without creating a visible wake-up

Pausing exactly when the final pixel leaves the viewport sounds precise, but it is not always the best visual behaviour. Some effects need a little time to resume before the user actually sees them again.

rootMargin lets you expand or contract the observer's effective root boundary. An effect that should wake before it reaches the viewport might use something like:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, {
  rootMargin: "200px 0px",
  threshold: 0,
});

That does not make 200px an optimal value. A CSS shimmer, a shader-heavy hero, and a scroll-linked sequence can all have different wake-up requirements.

Use the margin as an interaction decision, not a copied performance constant. The useful question is whether the effect can become active early enough that the user never sees it visibly restarting.

Thresholds need the same judgement. threshold: 0 works when any intersection should count, while another effect may only make sense once more of the element is visible. The observer tells you about geometry, not attention, so it should remain one production signal rather than becoming a proxy for everything the user is doing.

Keep the animation loop local to the component

A requestAnimationFrame example becomes unsafe in React if its mutable state lives at module scope. Two instances of the same component could end up sharing a running flag or frame ID, which means one instance can accidentally stop the other's loop.

Keep those values instance-local with refs:

import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export function useRafLoop(
  shouldAnimate: boolean,
  update: (delta: number) => void
) {
  const frameIdRef = useRef<number | null>(null);
  const previousTimeRef = useRef<number | null>(null);
  const updateRef = useRef(update);

  useEffect(() => {
    updateRef.current = update;
  }, [update]);

  const stop = useCallback(() => {
    if (frameIdRef.current !== null) {
      cancelAnimationFrame(frameIdRef.current);
      frameIdRef.current = null;
    }

    previousTimeRef.current = null;
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!shouldAnimate) {
      stop();
      return;
    }

    let active = true;

    const frame = (time: number) => {
      if (!active) return;

      if (previousTimeRef.current === null) {
        previousTimeRef.current = time;
      }

      const delta =
        time - previousTimeRef.current;

      previousTimeRef.current = time;

      updateRef.current(delta);

      frameIdRef.current =
        requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    };

    frameIdRef.current =
      requestAnimationFrame(frame);

    return () => {
      active = false;
      stop();
    };
  }, [shouldAnimate, stop]);
}

Each component instance now owns its own frame ID and previous timestamp. The effect cleanup also makes the loop tolerant of React development Strict Mode, where setup and cleanup may run an extra cycle to expose side-effect problems.

A component can combine the two hooks without letting viewport callbacks control the loop directly:

"use client";

import { useCallback } from "react";

export function AmbientCanvas() {
  const {
    ref,
    shouldAnimate,
    userPaused,
    setUserPaused,
  } = useAnimationGate({
    rootMargin: "200px 0px",
  });

  const update = useCallback((delta: number) => {
    // Advance your animation using delta.
  }, []);

  useRafLoop(shouldAnimate, update);

  return (
    <section ref={ref}>
      <canvas />

      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => {
          setUserPaused((paused) => !paused);
        }}
      >
        {userPaused ? "Resume animation" : "Pause animation"}
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

The observer updates inViewport. The Page Visibility API updates pageVisible. The media query updates motionAllowed. The button updates userPaused. None of those concerns owns the animation loop directly.

Pause the work, not only the pixels

Different animation technologies need different pause mechanics. Making a canvas invisible does not necessarily stop the code producing frames behind it.

For a manually managed requestAnimationFrame loop, stopping the scheduling path is the relevant operation. The hook above does that by cancelling the outstanding frame and refusing to create another until shouldAnimate becomes true again.

CSS animations have their own mechanism:

.ambient-shape {
  animation: drift 8s linear infinite;
}

.ambient-shape[data-paused="true"] {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}

The Web Animations API exposes pause() and play() on an Animation object, which is useful when timeline position needs to be preserved.

For WebGL or Three.js, the important question is whether the scene actually requires continuous rendering. If it owns a render loop, suspend that loop where appropriate rather than merely hiding the canvas.

The run gate can remain the same across all of these implementations. Only the adapter that translates shouldAnimate into engine behaviour needs to change.

Do not let resume create a time warp

Delta-time loops have one extra resume bug: the paused interval can become one enormous frame.

Suppose a canvas animation stores the previous frame timestamp, pauses for thirty seconds, then resumes while still comparing the new timestamp with the timestamp from before the pause. The next update may receive a huge delta.

A particle can jump across the screen, physics can advance too far, or easing logic can appear to snap because the implementation treated the entire paused interval as active animation time.

That is why the useRafLoop() example resets previousTimeRef when it stops. The first frame after resume establishes a fresh timestamp instead of trying to simulate all of the time that passed while the animation was inactive.

This is not a universal requirement for every animation engine. Timeline libraries may already preserve paused position correctly. Their documented lifecycle behaviour should remain the source of truth.

The larger decision is whether the effect should resume from its previous logical state or restart from the beginning. Ambient motion usually benefits from continuity. An entrance effect may reasonably restart under different circumstances. That behaviour should be chosen deliberately rather than becoming an accidental consequence of a visibility callback.

React cleanup is part of the optimization

An offscreen optimization is unfinished if observers, listeners, or render loops survive after the component that created them has unmounted. The page may stop displaying an effect while its background work continues.

Every side effect in the examples above owns its cleanup. IntersectionObserver is disconnected, visibilitychange is removed, the media-query listener is removed, and the component's outstanding animation frame is cancelled.

This matters on applications where sections appear conditionally or routes change without a full document reload. A motion-heavy site can otherwise accumulate work as users move through the experience.

For Next.js, APIs such as window, document, IntersectionObserver, and matchMedia() need to execute on the client. That does not mean every animation component in a Next.js project must be client-only. It means the code that directly depends on browser APIs needs the appropriate client boundary.

Reduced motion is an experience decision

prefers-reduced-motion is easy to misuse in performance code because honoring it often results in less animation work. Its purpose is still to represent a user's motion preference, so the resulting experience should be designed around that preference rather than treated as a cheap-device mode.

For a decorative looping background, reduced motion may mean showing a static visual state. For a transition that communicates a meaningful state change, a shorter or less spatial alternative may be more appropriate than removing every transition entirely.

The underlying information should remain available regardless of the animation path. Text should stay readable, controls should still operate, and required content should not depend on movement to become understandable.

It is also worth avoiding broad accessibility claims because a component responds to one media query. Reduced-motion handling addresses one part of motion accessibility. It does not prove that the component or page is fully accessible.

Test state transitions, not only the happy path

Most visibility bugs appear when states change in an order the implementation did not expect. A page can behave perfectly on first load and still fail once viewport state, tab state, user intent, and component lifecycle start interacting.

Test the animation after scrolling it out of view and back in. Switch to another tab while it is running and return. Manually pause it, scroll away, then come back and verify that the observer did not override the user's choice. If your implementation listens for motion-preference changes, test that path while the page is already open.

Unmount the component and confirm that no observer, listener, or frame loop survives. If the effect depends on expensive rendering, test the production build on the hardware you actually expect people to use, not only the development machine that authored the effect.

Pausing offscreen work is a useful production technique, but it does not prove that an effect is now cheap enough for every device. Profile the actual page before making performance claims.

How we treat offscreen motion at Hyperiux

Hyperiux Vault is a source-first library of creative interaction patterns for React and Next.js. Effects land as editable source in the project, so decisions around timing, rendering, responsive behaviour, reduced motion, and offscreen work can be inspected and adapted in the page where the interaction actually runs.

Different effects need different lifecycle strategies. A CSS text treatment does not carry the same rendering cost as a continuous WebGL scene, which is why our WebGL guidance includes pausing or limiting render loops when scenes are offscreen or the document is hidden.

If you are building a motion-heavy React or Next.js page, you can browse Hyperiux Vault effects. For continuously rendered scenes, the WebGL and 3D effects collection is the more relevant place to start.

Final takeaway

Offscreen animation becomes easier to reason about once viewport visibility stops owning playback directly. Keep viewport intersection, document visibility, reduced-motion preference, and user intent as separate states, then derive the single value the renderer actually needs.

That structure lets a CSS animation, requestAnimationFrame loop, Web Animations timeline, or WebGL scene use the same lifecycle policy without sharing the same implementation. It also gives resume behaviour, cleanup, and accessibility a clear place in the system instead of treating them as patches added after the animation already works.

articles.title: Nove classi per un pulsante: la mia piccola UI per canvas (e perché le voglio bene)
articles.description: Volevo un pulsante "Play" sul canvas del mio motore di gioco 2D. Un pulsante. Uno.  Poi ho aperto il...
articles.body_html:
Volevo un pulsante "Play" sul canvas del mio motore di gioco 2D.
Un pulsante. Uno.

Poi ho aperto il file e ho trovato questo:

import {
    BeeUI,
    BeeControl,
    BeePanel,
    BeeStack,
    BeeLabel,
    BeeUIButton,
    BEE_ANCHOR,
    BEE_UI_DEFAULTS,
    drawNineSlice
} from './src/ui/BeeUI.js';

Nove import per un menu di pausa. Ho riso anch'io. Poi ho capito che ognuno di quei nomi ha un motivo per esistere, e alla fine sono diventati la parte del motore che preferisco. Ve li presento uno per uno, con la serietà che si meritano (poca, ma sufficiente).

Il problema: il canvas non sa cos'è un pulsante

Il canvas HTML5 è un foglio bianco con i pixel. Non ha layout, non ha focus, non sa che il tuo menu dovrebbe restare centrato quando la finestra cambia dimensione. Tutto quello che il DOM ti regala gratis, sul canvas te lo devi costruire.

Quindi sì, servono un po' di classi.

BeeControl: il nonno di tutti

BeeControl è il nodo base. Non disegna niente (il suo draw() è letteralmente vuoto), ma sa fare le cose noiose e importanti:

  • tenere una lista di figli e un genitore (con campi privati #parent e #children, così nessuno li tocca a mano);
  • calcolare il proprio rettangolo a partire da ancore e offset;
  • capire se il mouse ci sta sopra con hit(x, y), partendo dall'ultimo figlio, cioè quello disegnato sopra.

Le ancore sono valori da 0 a 1 rispetto al genitore. Il conto è tutto qui:

const x = parentRect.x + parentRect.w * this.anchorLeft + this.offsetLeft;
const w = parentRect.w * (this.anchorRight - this.anchorLeft)
        + (this.offsetRight - this.offsetLeft);

Ancore uguali a sinistra e destra danno una larghezza fissa. Ancore diverse fanno allargare l'elemento insieme al genitore. Chi ha usato Godot riconoscerà il trucco, e non mi vergogno di averlo copiato.

BEE_ANCHOR: perché nessuno vuole scrivere setAnchors(1, 1, 1, 1)

Ricordarsi i numeri delle ancore è un incubo, quindi ci sono dei preset:

BEE_ANCHOR.TOP_LEFT, TOP, TOP_RIGHT,
LEFT, CENTER, RIGHT,
BOTTOM_LEFT, BOTTOM, BOTTOM_RIGHT,
FULL

Vuoi il punteggio in alto a destra con 16 pixel di margine?

new BeeLabel({ text: 'Score: 0', anchor: BEE_ANCHOR.TOP_RIGHT, x: 16, y: 16, width: 160 });

Ridimensioni la finestra e resta lì. Magia? No, sottrazioni.

BEE_UI_DEFAULTS: le decisioni che non voglio prendere ogni volta 

{ gap: 8, padding: 12, buttonWidth: 220, buttonHeight: 44 }

È un oggetto congelato con Object.freeze. Quattro numeri, zero discussioni. 44 pixel di altezza perché è una misura comoda da toccare col dito.

BeePanel: un rettangolo con ambizioni

BeePanel è un controllo che finalmente disegna qualcosa: colore di sfondo, bordo, angoli arrotondati (se il browser supporta roundRect) oppure un'immagine. E se gli passi anche slice, usa…

drawNineSlice: l'eroe silenzioso

Hai una cornice da 48×48 pixel e vuoi un pannello da 400×300 senza che gli angoli si deformino. La tecnica nine-slice taglia l'immagine in 9 pezzi: i 4 angoli restano fissi, i bordi si allungano in una sola direzione e il centro si allunga in tutte e due.

new BeePanel({
    anchor: BEE_ANCHOR.CENTER,
    width: 400, height: 300,
    image: frameImage,
    slice: { left: 12, top: 12, right: 12, bottom: 12 }
});

Nove chiamate a drawImage e il tuo menu sembra uscito da un gioco vero.

BeeStack: il flexbox dei poveri (e mi basta)

Mettere i pulsanti uno sotto l'altro calcolando le y a mano è il modo migliore per odiare la gamedev. BeeStack lo fa per te, in verticale ('v') o in orizzontale ('h'):

  • measure() somma le dimensioni dei figli visibili, più spazi e margini interni;
  • layout() li posiziona uno dopo l'altro;
  • se è ancorato al centro, si ricentra da solo in base alla dimensione calcolata.

BeeLabel e BeeUIButton: finalmente quello che volevo

BeeLabel scrive del testo. Fine. BeeUIButton è il pulsante vero: ha stati diversi per mouse sopra, premuto, disabilitato e focus, e si attiva al rilascio del mouse solo se sei ancora sopra al pulsante, esattamente come un pulsante del browser. Se ti penti a metà click, trascini fuori e non succede niente.

BeeUI: il capo

BeeUI è la radice dell'albero. Occupa tutto il canvas e a ogni frame:

  1. ricalcola il layout solo se qualcosa è cambiato (c'è un flag #dirty);
  2. gestisce hover e click del mouse;
  3. gestisce la tastiera: Tab e Shift+Tab, frecce o WASD, Invio e Spazio;
  4. gestisce il gamepad: croce direzionale e tasto A.

La parte che mi piace di più è focusToward(dx, dy). Quando premi "giù", non va semplicemente al pulsante successivo nella lista: cerca il controllo più vicino in quella direzione, penalizzando quelli troppo spostati di lato. Funziona anche con griglie di pulsanti, non solo con le liste.

Inoltre blocca il comportamento normale del Tab sul canvas, così il focus non scappa nella barra degli indirizzi a metà partita.

Un menu di pausa completo 

const ui = new BeeUI({ canvas });

const menu = ui.add(new BeeStack({ anchor: BEE_ANCHOR.CENTER, background: '#0f172acc', radius: 12 }));
menu.add(new BeeLabel({ text: 'PAUSA', align: 'center', font: 'bold 24px monospace' }));
menu.add(new BeeUIButton({ text: 'Riprendi', onClick: () => game.resume() }));
menu.add(new BeeUIButton({ text: 'Opzioni',  onClick: () => openOptions() }));
menu.add(new BeeUIButton({ text: 'Esci',     onClick: () => game.quit() }));
ui.focusAt(0);

// nel game loop
ui.update(input);
ui.draw(ctx);

Centrato, navigabile con mouse, tastiera e gamepad, e resta al suo posto quando ridimensioni la finestra. Il tutto in circa 700 righe senza dipendenze.

Quindi, nove classi erano troppe?

Probabilmente sì, per un pulsante.
Per un pulsante che si centra da solo, si allarga, si naviga col joystick e non si rompe quando giri il telefono, no.

E la prossima volta che qualcuno mi chiede "perché non usi semplicemente un <button> sopra il canvas?", gli mando questo articolo e vado a giocare.
